## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why does serving change the optimization priorities that made training successful?_

Training and serving pursue opposing operating objectives. Training maximizes aggregate throughput across large, scheduled batches and long runs, whereas serving must answer individual, heterogeneous requests under strict latency deadlines. Training amortizes hardware initialization and weight streaming across millions of examples; serving pays its full fixed cost on every query, and small inefficiencies accumulate into machine time that must be provisioned. A system handling one billion requests a day recovers more than eleven days of machine time every day from a single millisecond saved per request. Each request also runs inside a fixed end-to-end latency budget, in which network ingress, serialization, preprocessing, queueing, and postprocessing all spend time the model cannot use. When those stages consume most of the budget, kernel optimizations barely reach the user, and a prediction that arrives after the client has timed out has no value however accurate it is. Serving is therefore a capacity problem under uncontrolled traffic as much as a latency problem. Arrival rates swing between daily peaks and troughs, so capacity provisioned for the average collapses at the peak, while capacity provisioned for the peak sits idle and costly the rest of the day. The question a serving system answers is not whether the model computes correct outputs in isolation but whether it sustains reliable, low-latency execution under production variability. In D·A·M terms, serving is where the trained algorithm meets unpredictable live data inside the machine's latency budget, and all three constraints bind on every request.

## The Serving Inversion {#sec-model-serving-serving-paradigm-9634}

When a user uploads a photograph and waits for its label, or a chat interface sends a prompt and waits for the first word of the reply, each request carries a strict deadline of tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Every stage between the network socket and the response draws on that single allowance: decoding the payload, waiting in a queue, moving tensors to the accelerator, running the model, and formatting the answer. Moving from offline training to live traffic triggers the **serving inversion**\index{Serving inversion!definition}, a reversal of engineering priorities: training is judged by how much work the machine completes per hour, whereas serving is judged by whether each individual request returns before its deadline.

The benchmarks of @sec-benchmarking measured models under a load generator that decided when each request arrived. Production traffic has no such scheduler. Model **serving**\index{Serving!production deployment}\index{Model serving!paradigm shift} must sustain the operating targets that benchmarking evaluated under specified conditions while live traffic tests that operating envelope continuously, so measurement remains part of the service's lifecycle. In offline training, systems maximize aggregate throughput by packing large batches to amortize weight transfers from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and saturate matrix arithmetic units. In online serving, requests arrive stochastically from independent clients and must return within strict service-level objectives (SLOs). The primary engineering priority therefore inverts from long-run throughput to per-request latency. The inversion\index{Serving inversion!throughput-to-latency shift} restructures the balance of terms across both levels of the iron law of ML systems. Shrinking a task from a large training batch to small batches or individual inputs ($\BatchSize=1$) slashes the Data factor ($\text{Samples/Task}$ in @eq-intro-dam-iron-law) and inflates the Machine factor ($\text{Seconds/FLOP}$). The same shift appears across the unpacked terms of @eq-intro-iron-law ($\Time = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency$). For weight-dominated operations, small batches reduce arithmetic intensity and can shift execution from compute-bound matrix multiplications toward memory-bandwidth-bound transfers ($\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$). Simultaneously, the latency term $\Latency$\index{Latency!serving constraint} expands beyond microsecond accelerator kernel launches to include network transit, request serialization, and host orchestration, often becoming the binding constraint on end-to-end response time.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The multiplicative, additive, and pipelined formulations of the iron law of ML systems are established in @sec-introduction-iron-law-ml-systems-c32a.
:::

The inversion reshapes each D·A·M layer at once. In the data layer, the constraint shifts from total dataset volume to the arrival rate, payload freshness, and variable sequence dimensions of live queries. In the algorithm layer, execution becomes strictly forward-only: backpropagation state and optimizer memory vanish from the accelerator, even as dynamic input shapes introduce runtime execution variability into previously static operator graphs. In the machine layer, the operating target shifts from maximum hardware utilization to **headroom**\index{Headroom!tail latency}. Whereas offline training treats an idle accelerator as wasted capital, online serving treats near-saturation as an operational hazard, because stochastic request arrivals make queue lengths and waiting times diverge nonlinearly as utilization approaches 100 percent. Maintaining adequate headroom preserves the spare capacity needed to absorb transient traffic spikes without violating tail-latency percentiles, so serving optimizes completed requests under a strict latency deadline rather than steady-state hardware occupancy.

Meeting that latency deadline governs how engineering teams partition the end-to-end serving stack. A request's latency budget encompasses three sequential stages: host-side ingress and preprocessing (network termination, payload deserialization, and tokenization or feature transformation), accelerator kernel execution, and downstream postprocessing. Any millisecond consumed by unoptimized feature retrieval or queueing delays directly subtracts from the execution time allocated to the neural network itself. Consequently, the central engineering task in model serving is deciding which operations must remain on the synchronous request path, which tasks can be offloaded to asynchronous background pipelines, and how much headroom the system must reserve before tail-latency guarantees collapse under load. Three conditions therefore separate serving from the forward pass that a benchmark times: a per-request deadline, arrivals that no scheduler controls, and a stack in which the model is one stage among several.

::: {#dfn-model-serving-model-serving .callout-definition title="Model serving"}

***Model serving***\index{Model serving!definition} is the operational phase that provides model predictions to end-users or downstream systems under latency, throughput, availability, and cost constraints.

1.  **Significance**: Online serving turns training's priority on sustained hardware efficiency ($\EfficiencyHw$) into a request-latency constraint ($\EndToEndRequestLatency$), requiring a stack designed around the percentile named by its SLO.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike model training, which commonly processes scheduled batches, serving may handle stochastic online requests, synchronized streams, or offline batches.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that serving is "just the forward pass." In reality, it is a systems problem: model execution is only one component of a stack that may include request routing, load balancing, and data transformation.

:::

The SLO[^fn-slo-sla-serving] defines the latency target that shapes every architectural decision in the serving stack, establishing the strict time budget within which all request handling must complete. When an inference server receives a request, model execution represents only one segment of an end-to-end pipeline: network ingress, payload deserialization, feature transformation, queue scheduling, and output serialization all consume time before and after the accelerator runs. The end-to-end request lifecycle partitions execution into three sequential stages (@fig-serving-inference-pipeline): input preprocessing (traditional computing), neural network evaluation (deep learning), and output postprocessing with safety validation (traditional computing). Any of these stages can become the binding latency bottleneck. @Sec-model-serving-latency-budget-ef40 quantifies where the time goes and finds that host preprocessing can take longer than the forward pass itself.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ SLOs, service level agreements (SLAs), and the tail-latency percentiles they constrain are established in @sec-benchmarking-latency-tail-latency-5cde.
:::

[^fn-slo-sla-serving]: **SLOs in ML serving**\index{SLO!vs. SLA}\index{SLO!multidimensional targets}: An SLO is the internal target, as distinct from the contractual SLA. For ML serving, task quality and inference latency can both contribute to SLOs, creating multidimensional targets where improving one dimension (for example, deploying a larger model for accuracy) can violate another (latency).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: serving-lighthouses-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE CHAPTER'S TWO SERVICES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Running-case paragraph of @sec-model-serving-serving-paradigm-9634.
# │
# │ Goal: Introduce each lighthouse with the quantity that sets its regime.
# │ Show: ResNet-50 arithmetic and FP32 weight bytes per forward pass; GPT-2 XL
# │       FP16 weight bytes and the time to stream them once on an H100.
# │ How: Registry model and hardware entries.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *  # chapter-wide names (units, formatters) used by later cells
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, BYTES_FP16, BYTES_FP32, GB, MB, TB, second, millisecond
from mlsysim.core.units import GFLOPs, TFLOPs
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_flops, fmt_memory, fmt_time

class ServingLighthouses:
    """Regime-setting quantities for the ResNet-50 and GPT-2 XL services."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_flops = resnet.inference_flops
    resnet_weights = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    gpt2_weights = gpt2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    gpt2_read = (gpt2_weights / h100.memory.bandwidth).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(8.0 < resnet_flops.to("gigaflop").magnitude < 8.5, f"ResNet-50 should be ~8.2 GFLOP per image, got {resnet_flops}.")
    check(0.8 < gpt2_read.magnitude < 1.0, f"GPT-2 XL weight read should be ~0.9 ms on an H100, got {gpt2_read}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_gflops_str = fmt_flops(resnet_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_weights_mb_str = fmt_memory(resnet_weights, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    gpt2_weights_gb_str = fmt_memory(gpt2_weights, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt2_read_ms_str = fmt_time(gpt2_read, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
```

Two services carry the chapter, one per half, and each lighthouse arrives in the regime it represents. The first half follows a ResNet-50 image-classification service on one accelerator node. ResNet-50 is the book's compute-bound lighthouse. Each forward pass performs about `{python} ServingLighthouses.resnet_gflops_str` of arithmetic on `{python} ServingLighthouses.resnet_weights_mb_str` of FP32 weights, so a large training batch keeps the matrix units busy. A served request arrives alone, however, and at batch one the same forward pass spends most of its time on weight traffic and kernel launches rather than arithmetic. Recovering the efficiency that training enjoyed without breaking the deadline is the first half's problem, and the reference request profile introduced with the latency budget carries the service through queuing, batching, runtime selection, and replica startup. Large language model (LLM) serving then follows a GPT-2 XL chat service, the bandwidth-bound lighthouse whose decoding step @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1 traced. Each generated token streams all `{python} ServingLighthouses.gpt2_weights_gb_str` of its FP16 weights from memory, about `{python} ServingLighthouses.gpt2_read_ms_str` on the book's reference H100, so memory bandwidth sets token latency and the memory each conversation holds sets concurrency. Llama 3 8B, a larger member of the same transformer family, extends that case where the per-conversation cache grows large enough to bound how many requests share the accelerator. DLRM, the capacity-bound lighthouse, appears once as a contrast in which embedding lookups rather than arithmetic dominate a request, and MobileNetV2 appears where the target device cannot hold ResNet-50 at all.

| **Section**                      | **What it decides**                                                           | **Running case**                            | **Iron law term or resource it targets**                    |
|:---------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Serving System Architecture**  | How a replica turns arriving requests into accelerator work                   | ResNet-50 service                           | Fixed overhead $\Latency$ (protocol, serialization, copies) |
| **Request Lifecycle**            | Where one request's latency budget goes                                       | ResNet-50 request; DLRM contrast            | Every term, stage by stage                                  |
| **Queuing Theory**               | How much headroom many concurrent requests need                               | ResNet-50 capacity plan                     | Queueing delay added to $\Latency$                          |
| **Throughput Optimization**      | How many requests share each weight read                                      | ResNet-50 batching sweep                    | $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$ and $\Latency$ per request         |
| **Inference Runtime Selection**  | Which engine and number format execute a batch                                | ResNet-50 runtimes and precisions           | Hardware efficiency $\EfficiencyHw$ and bytes $\DataVolume$ |
| **Node-Level Optimization**      | What stalls the path between network socket and accelerator                   | ResNet-50 node profile                      | Host-side $\Latency$                                        |
| **Model Loading and Versioning** | How fast a new replica serves, and whether it computes what training computed | ResNet-50 cold start and preprocessing skew | Startup time and prediction accuracy                        |
| **LLM Serving**                  | How token streams share memory bandwidth and capacity                         | GPT-2 XL decode; Llama 3 8B cache           | $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$ per token; memory capacity         |
| **Economics and Planning**       | How many accelerators, at what cost per completed request                     | ResNet-50 fleet; Llama 3 8B tokens          | Cost per request that meets the SLO                         |

: **Chapter Map**: Each section answers one serving decision on one of the running cases and names the iron law term or resource that decision most affects. The first four rows follow a single ResNet-50 replica from its architecture to batching; the remaining rows change what the replica executes, how it starts, what it produces, and what it costs. {#tbl-model-serving-chapter-spine tbl-colwidths="[22,32,22,24]"}

The architecture section (@tbl-model-serving-chapter-spine) examines the inference server that sits between the network and the accelerator. The request lifecycle then traces one ResNet-50 request through that server and finds that the model is one slice of its latency budget. Queuing theory lets many requests arrive at once and derives the headroom that keeps their tail latency bounded, and throughput optimization raises each replica's service rate by batching, where the chapter's first half ends. The second half changes what each replica runs and how it starts. Runtime and precision selection decide how fast a batch executes, node-level optimization removes the stalls between host and accelerator, and model loading decides how quickly a new replica can serve and whether it computes what training computed. LLM serving then replaces fixed outputs with token streams, and economics and planning converts the whole stack into accelerator count and cost per request. Two placement decisions precede all of these: the first is temporal, whether predictions are computed ahead of time or on demand, and the second is spatial, where the model physically runs.

### Static vs. dynamic inference {#sec-model-serving-static-vs-dynamic-inference-e864}

A nightly job that precomputes product recommendations for existing users can pack thousands of items into each accelerator batch, whereas a live content-moderation API must score an uploaded image within milliseconds of arrival. Deciding whether to generate predictions before or during a user request sets the trade-off between offline hardware efficiency and online responsiveness [@google2024staticdynamic]. It determines whether an accelerator runs in an unconstrained throughput regime or under the strict tail-latency deadlines of an interactive serving loop.

#### Static inference {#sec-model-serving-static-inference-35f4}

Static inference\index{Static inference!precomputed predictions} (also called offline or batch inference) precomputes predictions for anticipated inputs and stores them in a retrieval store. Moving model execution entirely out of the user request path alters the underlying hardware constraints. Because batch jobs have no millisecond-level deadlines, accelerators can use large batches ($\BatchSize\gg 1$) selected for throughput within memory limits. Reusing weights across samples raises arithmetic intensity for weight-dominated operations. A batch-size sweep identifies where throughput stops improving. When a client issues a request (for example, a user opening nightly generated recommendation rankings), the serving system performs a low-latency key-value lookup rather than executing a forward pass on an accelerator. The primary operational constraint shifts from accelerator latency to storage capacity and data freshness. Precomputing predictions across an entire input domain scales combinatorially ($\mathcal{O}(\RecommenderUserCount\times \RecommenderItemCount)$ for $\RecommenderUserCount$ users and $\RecommenderItemCount$ items in recommendation systems), and stale predictions persist until the next batch refresh.

#### Dynamic inference {#sec-model-serving-dynamic-inference-d2d5}

**Dynamic inference**\index{Dynamic inference!definition}\index{Online inference|see{Dynamic inference}} (also called online or real-time inference) evaluates inputs on demand as requests arrive. On-demand execution accommodates arbitrary, previously unseen inputs within the model schema and immediately reflects newly deployed model weights without requiring precomputation. However, executing the model directly within the user request path subjects inference to the strict end-to-end latency budget set by its SLO. Because user requests arrive stochastically, the serving runtime cannot delay execution indefinitely to accumulate large batches. Serving requests individually or in small batches ($\BatchSize=1$ to $\BatchSize=4$) can expose weight traffic or launch overhead that larger batches amortize. When these costs bind execution, the device completes fewer queries per unit time, increasing provisioned cost per query. This tension between interactive response time and hardware efficiency can make dynamic serving more expensive per query than offline batching (example \ref{exmp-cost-latency}).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cost-latency-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST OF LATENCY CALCULATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "The Cost of Latency" (Serving Paradigm section)
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the economic trade-off between response time and hardware bill.
# │ Show: That batch one costs several times more per query than batch eight
# │       for almost the same latency.
# │ How: ResNet-50 eager FP16 profile on the H100 at batch 1 and batch 8.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Infrastructure
from mlsysim.engine.serving_profile import resnet50_h100_profile
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_usd, fmt_time, fmt_rate

class CostLatencyCalc:
    """Quantifies the economic trade-off between latency and hardware cost per million queries."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpu_cost_per_hour_value = Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuTrainingPerHour.rate
    _p = resnet50_h100_profile()  # the chapter's ResNet-50 reference profile
    latency_a_ms_value = _p.eager_fp16(1).to(ms)
    throughput_a_rps_value = (1 * count / latency_a_ms_value).to(count / second)
    latency_b_ms_value = _p.eager_fp16(8).to(ms)
    throughput_b_rps_value = (8 * count / latency_b_ms_value).to(count / second)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    queries_per_hour_a_value = (throughput_a_rps_value * hour).to(count)
    cost_per_million_a_value = (gpu_cost_per_hour_value * hour) / (queries_per_hour_a_value / (MILLION * count))
    queries_per_hour_b_value = (throughput_b_rps_value * hour).to(count)
    cost_per_million_b_value = (gpu_cost_per_hour_value * hour) / (queries_per_hour_b_value / (MILLION * count))
    cost_increase_pct_value = (cost_per_million_a_value / cost_per_million_b_value - 1) * 100
    cost_ratio_value = cost_per_million_a_value / cost_per_million_b_value

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(cost_ratio_value > 1, "Scenario A (low latency) must cost more per query than Scenario B.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpu_cost_per_hour_str = fmt_usd(gpu_cost_per_hour_value, precision=0, commas=False, per="hour")
    latency_a_ms_str = fmt_time(latency_a_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=1, commas=False)
    throughput_a_rps_str = fmt_rate(round(throughput_a_rps_value.magnitude) * (count / second), 'req/s', precision=0, commas=True)
    latency_b_ms_str = fmt_time(latency_b_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=1, commas=False)
    throughput_b_rps_str = fmt_rate(round(throughput_b_rps_value.magnitude) * (count / second), 'req/s', precision=0, commas=True)
    cost_a_str = fmt_usd(cost_per_million_a_value, precision=2, commas=False)
    cost_b_str = fmt_usd(cost_per_million_b_value, precision=2, commas=False)
    cost_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(cost_ratio_value), precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#exmp-cost-latency .callout-example title="The cost of latency"}

Latency constraints directly dictate infrastructure costs. The figures below come from the ResNet-50 reference profile that @sec-model-serving-batching-helps-f1dc later sweeps across batch sizes. Consider a GPU server renting for `{python} CostLatencyCalc.gpu_cost_per_hour_str`.

Scenario A (low latency): Batch size 1.

*   Latency: `{python} CostLatencyCalc.latency_a_ms_str`.
*   Throughput: `{python} CostLatencyCalc.throughput_a_rps_str`.
*   Cost per million queries: `{python} CostLatencyCalc.cost_a_str`.

Scenario B (high throughput): Batch size 8.

*   Latency: `{python} CostLatencyCalc.latency_b_ms_str`, barely above batch one, because the fixed launch cost dominates both.
*   Throughput: `{python} CostLatencyCalc.throughput_b_rps_str`.
*   Cost per million queries: `{python} CostLatencyCalc.cost_b_str`.

**Systems insight**: Serving one image at a time saves only the difference between `{python} CostLatencyCalc.latency_b_ms_str` and `{python} CostLatencyCalc.latency_a_ms_str` of latency, yet multiplies the hardware cost per million queries by `{python} CostLatencyCalc.cost_ratio_mult_str`. Engineers must quantify whether that speedup generates enough business value to justify the `{python} CostLatencyCalc.cost_ratio_mult_str` cost increase.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: resnet-h100-profile-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESNET-50 SERVING PROFILE ON ONE H100
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The chapter's reference profile; every later ResNet-50 serving
# │          cell (latency budget, queueing, capacity plan, batching sweep,
# │          runtime and precision comparisons, cost) reads it.
# │
# │ Goal: Model one ResNet-50 forward pass on the reference H100 per serving
# │       engine and batch size, from the iron law's additive terms.
# │ Show: Eager batch-one latency is overhead-bound; batching and compiled
# │       engines remove the overhead; INT8 matters at batch, not at batch one.
# │ How: time = kernels x host issue cost + kernels x per-kernel device floor
# │      + weight read + batch x per-image device time. Per-image FP16 time
# │      uses the training chapter's sustained fraction (the registry's A100
# │      ResNet-50 training rate); per-image INT8 time is the MLPerf Inference v5.0 measured rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models, Ops, Literature, BYTES_FP16, BYTES_INT8, BYTES_FP32
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, second, millisecond, microsecond
from mlsysim.engine.serving_profile import resnet50_h100_profile
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_time, fmt_rate, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple, fmt_math

class ResNetH100Profile:
    """ResNet-50 on one H100: modeled forward-pass time per engine and batch size."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # The shared model (mlsysim.engine.serving_profile) is the single source; the
    # compression chapter's INT8 deployment profile calls the same function.
    _p = resnet50_h100_profile()
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    python_dispatch = _p.python_dispatch
    kernel_launch = _p.kernel_launch
    kernel_floor = _p.kernel_floor
    eager_kernels = _p.eager_kernels
    fused_kernels = _p.fused_kernels
    int8_offline_img_s = _p.int8_offline_img_s

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    sustained_fraction = _p.sustained_fraction
    per_image_fp16 = _p.per_image_fp16
    per_image_int8 = _p.per_image_int8
    per_image_tf32 = _p.per_image_tf32
    weights_fp16 = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    weights_int8 = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    weight_read_fp16 = _p.weight_read_fp16
    weight_read_int8 = _p.weight_read_int8
    weight_read_fp32 = _p.weight_read_fp32
    eager_issue = (eager_kernels * (python_dispatch + kernel_launch)).to(millisecond)
    eager_b1 = _p.eager_fp16(1)
    eager_fixed = _p.eager_fp16(0)
    eager_per_image = per_image_fp16.to(millisecond)
    overhead_share_b1 = (eager_issue / eager_b1).to("").magnitude
    torchscript_b1 = _p.torchscript_fp16(1)
    onnx_b1 = _p.onnx_fp16(1)
    trt_fp32_b1 = _p.tensorrt("fp32", 1)
    trt_fp16_b1 = _p.tensorrt("fp16", 1)
    trt_int8_b1 = _p.tensorrt("int8", 1)
    trt_fp16_b16 = _p.tensorrt("fp16", 16)
    eager_ceiling_img_s = _p.large_batch_throughput("fp16")
    tf32_ceiling_img_s = _p.large_batch_throughput("fp32")
    int8_ceiling_img_s = int8_offline_img_s

    def eager_ms(batch, _fixed=eager_fixed, _per=eager_per_image):
        return (_fixed + batch * _per).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.245 < sustained_fraction < 0.26, f"Sustained fraction must match the training chapter (~0.25), got {sustained_fraction:.3f}.")
    check(3.4 < eager_b1.magnitude < 3.7, f"Eager batch-one forward pass should be about 3.5 ms, got {eager_b1}.")
    check(overhead_share_b1 > 0.7, "Eager batch one must be overhead-bound: host issue dominates.")
    check(eager_b1 > torchscript_b1 > onnx_b1 > trt_fp16_b1 > trt_int8_b1, "Each engine must remove overhead the previous one paid.")
    check((trt_fp16_b1 - trt_int8_b1) / trt_fp16_b1 < 0.15, "At batch one INT8 should barely beat FP16: the kernel floor dominates.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    eager_b1_ms_str = fmt_time(eager_b1, "millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    eager_issue_ms_str = fmt_time(eager_issue, "millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    overhead_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(overhead_share_b1, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    eager_kernels_str = fmt(eager_kernels, precision=0, commas=False)
    fused_kernels_str = fmt(fused_kernels, precision=0, commas=False)
    per_image_fp16_us_str = fmt_time(round(per_image_fp16.magnitude) * microsecond, "microsecond", precision=0, commas=False)
    per_image_int8_us_str = fmt_time(round(per_image_int8.magnitude) * microsecond, "microsecond", precision=0, commas=False)
    kernel_floor_us_str = fmt_time(kernel_floor, "microsecond", precision=0, commas=False)
    dispatch_us_str = fmt_time(python_dispatch, "microsecond", precision=0, commas=False)
    launch_us_str = fmt_time(kernel_launch, "microsecond", precision=0, commas=False)
    sustained_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(sustained_fraction, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    int8_offline_str = fmt_rate(round(int8_offline_img_s, -2), "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    eager_ceiling_str = fmt_rate(round(eager_ceiling_img_s, -2), "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    eager_fixed_ms_str = fmt_time(eager_fixed, "millisecond", precision=2, commas=False)
    eager_per_image_ms_str = fmt_time(eager_per_image, "millisecond", precision=3, commas=False)
    affine_math = fmt_math(
        rf"\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = {eager_fixed.magnitude:.2f}\text{{ ms}} + ({eager_per_image.magnitude:.3f}\text{{ ms}})\,\BatchSize"
    )
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: static-batch-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STATIC VS DYNAMIC INFERENCE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Static vs Dynamic inference narrative (photo organization example)
# │
# │ Goal: Contrast the economics of static vs. dynamic inference.
# │ Show: That static precomputation is superior for predictable inputs.
# │ How: Compare total batch time to per-request latency for photo classification.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_count, fmt_time, check

class StaticBatchCalc:
    """Contrasts static vs. dynamic inference economics for photo classification."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_photos_value = 10_000  # photos in user library
    inference_ms_value = ResNetH100Profile.eager_b1  # batch-one forward pass, reference profile
    offline_img_s = ResNetH100Profile.int8_offline_img_s  # measured large-batch rate
    dynamic_latency_budget_ms_value = 100 * ms  # scenario assumption: real-time latency budget

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    serial_total_s_value = (n_photos_value * inference_ms_value).to(second)
    batch_total_s_value = (n_photos_value / (offline_img_s / second)).to(second)
    speedup_value = (serial_total_s_value / batch_total_s_value).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(batch_total_s_value < 1 * second < serial_total_s_value, "Batched pass must take under a second; one at a time, tens of seconds.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_photos_str = fmt_count(n_photos_value, label="photo")
    inference_ms_str = fmt_time(inference_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=1, commas=False)
    serial_total_s_str = fmt_time(round(serial_total_s_value.magnitude) * second, 'second', precision=0, commas=False)
    batch_total_s_str = fmt_time(batch_total_s_value, 'second', precision=2, commas=False)
    speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(speedup_value, -1), precision=0, commas=True)
    dynamic_latency_budget_ms_str = fmt_time(dynamic_latency_budget_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=False)
```

Consider two contrasting deployment scenarios for a ResNet-50 image classifier. A static batch approach suits a photo management application that preclassifies every image in a user library overnight. Classifying `{python} StaticBatchCalc.n_photos_str` one at a time, at `{python} StaticBatchCalc.inference_ms_str` per batch-one forward pass on the reference H100, would take `{python} StaticBatchCalc.serial_total_s_str`. At the `{python} ResNetH100Profile.int8_offline_str` that MLPerf Inference [@reddi2020] measured for a compiled INT8 engine at large batch on the same accelerator, the same library takes `{python} StaticBatchCalc.batch_total_s_str`, about `{python} StaticBatchCalc.speedup_mult_str` faster. Clients then experience instantaneous retrieval upon browsing. Conversely, a dynamic online approach suits a content moderation service that must evaluate user-uploaded media in real time, where each image traverses the complete preprocessing, accelerator execution, and postprocessing pipeline within a `{python} StaticBatchCalc.dynamic_latency_budget_ms_str` service-level objective.

These two modes optimize for different operating regimes. Static inference maximizes accelerator utilization and amortizes memory transfers across large, offline batches, trading persistent storage capacity for zero serving latency at query time. Dynamic inference minimizes tail latency under stochastic, concurrent traffic, accepting lower compute efficiency and higher marginal cost per query to evaluate arbitrary, unpredictable inputs. Production architectures frequently combine both paradigms in a tiered design. Static precomputation populates key-value caches with predictions for high-frequency queries, such as catalog items or viral media, while dynamic serving clusters evaluate the long tail of novel or personalized requests. Deciding when predictions are computed resolves only the temporal dimension of serving, however. Equally binding is the spatial dimension, where the model physically executes, because physical placement dictates memory hierarchy limits, network boundaries, and the hardware budget available to the serving stack.

### The spectrum of serving architectures {#sec-model-serving-spectrum-serving-architectures-8966}

A cloud server can pool accelerators behind an HTTP endpoint at the cost of a network round trip and multi-second cold starts, whereas a hearing aid or industrial sensor microcontroller cannot afford a network hop or an operating system at all. Although "serving" often implies a networked server processing API requests, the four deployment paradigms (Cloud, Edge, Mobile, and TinyML) and the physical constraints that give rise to them—the light barrier, the power wall, and the memory wall—shape the serving stack into different forms. Serving spans a continuum. At the cloud end, **centralized networked microservices**\index{Microservice!cloud model serving} pool accelerators to optimize throughput and cost per query, at the expense of network round-trip overhead and cold-start latency. Further along, **application-embedded edge serving**\index{Edge serving!embedded function calls} runs models inside client processes via direct function calls, which eliminates network latency and preserves privacy at the expense of strict device memory and power limits. At the far end, **bare-metal firmware execution**\index{TinyML!bare-metal serving} runs on microcontrollers. Those hardware limits do not disappear at serving time; serving adds latency SLOs and cost pressure on top of limits that training could absorb through patience. The same model may therefore require different serving strategies depending on where it runs.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The light barrier, power wall, and memory wall that give rise to the four deployment paradigms are established in @sec-ml-systems-deployment-spectrum-71be.
:::

The three architectures differ in what binds. Networked serving\index{Serving!cloud/data center}\index{Microservice!model serving} runs the model as a standalone service behind HTTP or gRPC, so network transfer and serialization join model execution as candidate bottlenecks. Data-center accelerators support batching and concurrency, but a new replica's cold start\index{Cold start!cloud serving} can stretch from seconds to minutes because container startup, model loading, and warmup sit outside the steady-state request path. Application-embedded serving\index{Serving!mobile/edge}\index{Serving!edge inference, embedded serving} runs the model inside the user's application process on a phone or embedded board, behind a function call rather than a network interface. With no shared server to batch for, optimization targets energy and responsiveness (the shape that benchmarking calls SingleStream), and a passively cooled envelope of a few watts throttles sustained inference once the chassis heats. Bare-metal serving\index{Serving!TinyML} compiles the model into microcontroller firmware, often without an operating system or a dynamic allocator, so weights execute in place from flash memory and activations fit a preallocated tensor arena\index{Tensor arena!TinyML memory} of a few hundred kilobytes of SRAM. Batching is impossible on a single sensor stream.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The MLPerf SingleStream, MultiStream, Server, and Offline scenarios are established in @sec-benchmarking-mlperf-execution-scenarios-89f0.
:::

Embedded execution enables **zero-copy inference**\index{Inference!zero-copy, mobile optimization}. When data moves through a system, each copy consumes CPU cycles and memory bandwidth. In cloud serving, separate physical memory spaces force repeated transfers. A camera frame passes from a network socket buffer to user space, through a preprocessing buffer into page-locked host DRAM, and across PCIe into accelerator memory. A mobile pipeline can eliminate these intermediate copies when its camera, image signal processor (ISP), CPU, and NPU exchange shared buffer descriptors in unified system memory. In unified-memory system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, such as Apple A- and M-series processors or Qualcomm Snapdragon, all compute engines share a single physical DRAM pool. When software passes buffer handles rather than duplicating bytes, inference latency drops and memory bus power decreases, although format conversions may still require CPU or ISP intervention.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: resnet-spectrum-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESNET-50 ACROSS THE SERVING SPECTRUM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "ResNet-50 Across the Serving Spectrum"
# │
# │ Goal: Contrast serving requirements across Cloud, Mobile, and TinyML.
# │ Show: That the same model requires different formats and architectures.
# │ How: Calculate model sizes and compare NPU vs. CPU efficiency.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_time, fmt_rate, fmt_memory, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_energy

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class ResNetServingSpectrum:
    """
    Namespace for ResNet-50 Serving Spectrum comparison.
    Scenario: Mapping the same architecture (or alternatives) to Cloud, Mobile, TinyML.
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    m_resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    m_mobilenet = Models.Vision.MobileNetV2

    s_cloud = Platforms.Cloud
    s_mobile = Platforms.Mobile
    s_tiny = Platforms.Tiny

    # Cloud: TensorRT FP16 engine on the reference H100, from the chapter's profile
    P = ResNetH100Profile
    cloud_inf_b1_ms = P.trt_fp16_b1
    cloud_inf_b16_ms = P.trt_fp16_b16
    cloud_throughput = round(P.eager_ceiling_img_s, -2)  # FP16 large-batch ceiling at the sustained fraction
    cloud_vram = 2 * GB  # scenario assumption: batch-32 engine residency

    # Mobile (Smartphone) Performance
    mobile_inf_npu_ms = 12.0
    mobile_inf_cpu_ms = 45.0
    mobile_throughput = 80
    mobile_energy_npu = 0.8 * mJ  # scenario assumption: per-image mobile NPU energy
    mobile_energy_cpu = 4.2 * mJ  # scenario assumption: per-image mobile CPU energy

    # TinyML (Cortex-M7) Performance
    tiny_inf_ms = 120.0
    tiny_energy = 12.0 * mJ  # scenario assumption: per-image TinyML energy

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Step 1: Calculate sizes using the Digital Twins
    cloud_size = m_resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    mobile_size = m_resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    tiny_original = m_resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    tiny_alt = m_mobilenet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)

    # Step 2: TinyML feasibility check
    tiny_feasibility = tiny_original < s_tiny.ram

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        not tiny_feasibility,
        f"ResNet-50 ({fmt_memory(tiny_original, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)}) should NOT fit on TinyML (<{fmt_memory(s_tiny.ram, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)}).",
    )
    check(mobile_energy_cpu >= mobile_energy_npu * 3, "NPU should be significantly more energy efficient than CPU.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # System names
    cloud_name_str = MarkdownStr(s_cloud.name)
    mobile_name_str = MarkdownStr(s_mobile.name)
    tiny_name_str = MarkdownStr(s_tiny.name)

    cloud_model_mb_str = fmt_memory(cloud_size, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=True)
    cloud_inf_b1_ms_str = fmt_time(cloud_inf_b1_ms, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    cloud_inf_b16_ms_str = fmt_time(cloud_inf_b16_ms, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    cloud_throughput_img_per_s_str = fmt_rate(cloud_throughput, 'img/s', precision=0, commas=True)
    cloud_vram_gb_str = fmt_memory(cloud_vram, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)

    mobile_model_mb_str = fmt_memory(mobile_size, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=True)
    mobile_inf_npu_ms_str = fmt_time(mobile_inf_npu_ms, 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=False)
    mobile_inf_cpu_ms_str = fmt_time(mobile_inf_cpu_ms, 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=False)
    mobile_throughput_img_per_s_str = fmt_rate(mobile_throughput, 'img/s', precision=0, commas=False)
    mobile_energy_npu_mj_str = fmt_energy(mobile_energy_npu, unit=mJ, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobile_energy_cpu_mj_str = fmt_energy(mobile_energy_cpu, unit=mJ, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobile_mem_mb_str = fmt_memory(150 * MB, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)

    tiny_model_mb_str = fmt_memory(tiny_original, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=True)
    tiny_alt_mb_str = fmt_memory(tiny_alt, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=True)
    tiny_inf_ms_str = fmt_time(tiny_inf_ms, 'millisecond', precision=0, commas=False)
    tiny_throughput_str = fmt_rate(8, "img/s", precision=0, commas=False)
    tiny_arena_kb_str = fmt_memory(320 * KB, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    tiny_sram_kb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(s_tiny.ram, unit=s_tiny.ram.units, precision=0, commas=True)
    tiny_energy_mj_str = fmt_energy(tiny_energy, unit=mJ, precision=0, commas=False)
```

The deployment tiers differ first in their operating envelopes (latency targets, memory, and power), which @sec-ml-systems-deployment-spectrum-71be derived and tabulated for each paradigm. What serving adds is the model each tier can actually run. Applying those envelopes to one image-classification workload, @tbl-resnet-serving-spectrum shows why cloud and mobile can adapt ResNet-50 while TinyML must substitute MobileNetV2. The cloud column runs the model through TensorRT, NVIDIA's ahead-of-time inference compiler,[^fn-tensorrt-gpu-serving] and the mobile column through the TensorFlow Lite runtime. The chapter uses these engines as given until @sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef examines what such runtimes do to a model.

[^fn-tensorrt-gpu-serving]: **TensorRT**\index{TensorRT!GPU optimization}: TensorRT builds its engine ahead of time for one microarchitecture (such as Hopper or Blackwell) [@nvidia2024tensorrt]. That target-specific build phase allows the compiler to generate fused kernels, select microarchitecture-specific Tensor Core execution paths, and optimize memory layouts (such as NC/32HW32). The resulting nonportable engine reduces per-request execution latency and minimizes the accelerator count needed to satisfy a target throughput.

**Systems insight**: It is tempting to read @tbl-resnet-serving-spectrum as one model deployed three ways. That reading is misleading: the cloud and mobile tiers share the ResNet-50 graph but use different precision and runtimes, while the TinyML tier cannot run ResNet-50 at all and substitutes an architecture designed for its constraints. Treating these as one model hides the work that makes each deployment possible.

:::

Whichever tier hosts it, a networked deployment runs the model inside a server process, and each such replica must turn an irregular stream of requests into work its accelerator can execute efficiently. That conversion is the job of the inference server's internal architecture.

## Serving System Architecture {#sec-model-serving-serving-system-architecture-4879}

Inside each replica, user requests arrive in irregular bursts—milliseconds apart one moment and silent for seconds the next—whereas accelerator compute engines demand steady streams of uniform, dense batches to saturate memory bandwidth and arithmetic units. Reconciling these two incompatible rhythms at the system boundary requires a serving architecture that decouples network ingress from execution scheduling, absorbing arrival bursts and packing irregular inputs into dense batches without violating latency SLOs.

### Internal architecture and request flow {#sec-model-serving-anatomy-inference-server-f12e}

If a web server invoked the accelerator synchronously every time a socket read completed, slow client uploads would stall the GPU and concurrent connections would contend for device memory. An inference server\index{Inference server!architecture}[^fn-inference-server-serving] (such as NVIDIA Triton or TensorFlow Serving) avoids this by acting as a specialized runtime scheduler that manages concurrency, device memory, and data movement between host CPUs and accelerator devices. Rather than running the model directly on the network thread, the server pipelines incoming requests through dedicated subsystems that isolate client network handling from accelerator compute. Every request traverses a six-stage runtime pipeline (@fig-server-anatomy) from network ingress and request-buffering queues through the dynamic batcher to the inference runner and hardware accelerator.

[^fn-inference-server-serving]: **Inference server**\index{Inference server!serving architecture}: Google's TensorFlow Serving\index{TensorFlow Serving!inference server} [@olston2017tensorflow] helped establish the separation of model logic from serving infrastructure; NVIDIA's Triton\index{Triton!inference server} [@nvidia_triton] extends this pattern across multiple model frameworks and backends. The critical design insight is that a scheduler and dynamic batcher turn irregular single-request traffic into accelerator-friendly execution, improving utilization when latency budgets allow batching. Exact utilization gains depend on model, hardware, arrival rate, and the configured batching window.

::: {#fig-server-anatomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Inference Server Anatomy**: A modern inference server decouples network handling from accelerator execution through a staged pipeline. Each stage isolates a concern, from absorbing bursty traffic to forming efficient batches, so the hardware accelerator stays busy despite irregular arrival patterns." fig-alt="Flowchart showing a six-stage inference server pipeline: client to network ingress to request queue to dynamic batcher, then down to inference runner to accelerator. Arrows connect stages sequentially."}
