- [ ] **Adaptive windows**: For a desired expected batch count, explain why higher traffic permits a shorter formation window. How would you check whether the realized batches can keep up with arrivals, and what must a load test verify before accepting the configuration?
- [ ] **When not to batch**: Name a latency target, runtime limitation, or memory condition under which a batching window of zero is the right configuration.
- [ ] **Bytes and joules per image**: Using @tbl-model-serving-resnet-batch-bytes, explain why energy per image falls steeply from batch 1 to batch 8 but only slightly from batch 8 to batch 32.
- [ ] **The first half in one request**: For one ResNet-50 request arriving at 500 QPS, name the stage that sets its latency floor, the quantity that sizes the queue's headroom, and the two things the scheduler's batch changes, and explain how each depends on the one before it.

:::

## Inference Runtime Selection {#sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef}

Running an unchanged ResNet-50 model through a compiled C++ engine rather than an eager Python interpreter cuts batch-one latency on the reference H100 by more than fivefold, without altering a single weight. Dynamic batching and request scheduling govern how requests are grouped and queued, but an execution engine still has to map the resulting tensor operations onto physical execution units and memory hierarchies. The **inference runtime**\index{Inference runtime!execution engine}, the software layer that schedules tensor operations and manages device resources, therefore changes both latency and throughput for a fixed model architecture. Runtime engineering proceeds in two steps: selection chooses the execution engine that fits the deployment target, and configuration tunes that engine for the model, hardware, input shapes, and latency budget.

### Runtime constraint map {#sec-ml-frameworks-quantitative-framework-efficiency-comparison-3b77}

Attempting to deploy a Python-based server runtime onto a 256 KB microcontroller fails before the first request arrives, and exporting a model with custom operators to a mobile neural processing unit (NPU) delegate can silently push unsupported layers back onto the CPU. The deployment target\index{Deployment target!cloud to edge spectrum} narrows the viable runtime family before any speed comparison matters, and each tier in @tbl-resnet-serving-spectrum rules out entire classes of software. The keyword-spotting microcontroller in @sec-ml-frameworks-tinyml-micro-runtimes-2a1b requires a fixed memory arena and a compact C/C++ runtime. A smartphone, by contrast, can host an application runtime that routes supported operators to accelerator delegates and falls back to another path when an operator is missing. Within each target envelope, @tbl-framework-efficiency-matrix lists the candidate runtime families and the conversion or execution condition each candidate must pass before latency or memory numbers can be compared.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
```

| **Runtime family**              | **Where it fits**              | **Constraint anchor**                                             | **Optimization path**                         | **Constraint to test**                     |
|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| **PyTorch eager**               | Research and iteration         | Baseline latency; full Python/runtime footprint                   | Dynamic graphs, eager debugging               | Dispatch overhead and missing graph view   |
| **Compiled PyTorch/TensorFlow** | Server training and serving    | Workload-dependent gains when graph capture is clean              | Graph capture, fusion, layout planning        | Operator coverage and graph breaks         |
| **TensorFlow Lite/Core ML**     | Mobile and edge inference      | Target-specific mobile latency and package-size budgets           | Quantization, static graphs, NPU delegates    | Target-specific conversion constraints     |
| **TF Lite Micro/microTVM**      | Microcontroller inference      | Target-specific microcontroller RAM and flash budgets             | Static allocation, INT8 kernels               | Selected operators and constrained memory  |
| **ONNX Runtime**                | Cross-framework serving        | Backend-dependent; can match native runtimes for supported graphs | Standard graph format, execution providers    | Export gaps and custom-operator fallbacks  |
| **TensorRT/TVM**                | Hardware-specialized inference | Target-dependent gains over untuned eager baselines               | Kernel fusion, precision lowering, autotuning | Narrower target and conversion assumptions |

: **Runtime Constraint Map**: Read each row left to right as one trade, in which a family gives up flexibility, gains an optimization path, and acquires a new way to fail. The middle column records where a family sits relative to an untuned eager baseline rather than a measured result, so latency, memory use, energy, and utilization still have to be measured for the specific model, hardware, precision, batch size, and compiler configuration. {#tbl-framework-efficiency-matrix tbl-colwidths="[17,18,25,19,21]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

A runtime can fit the device and still fail to execute the exported model. Specialized inference runtimes such as TensorRT\index{TensorRT!hardware utilization} and Apache TVM\index{Apache TVM!ML compiler} require compatible operators and conversion paths; a mobile delegate may support only part of a graph. Unsupported regions can introduce fallback execution and extra transfers. Portability therefore requires an agreement about the graph and operator semantics on both sides of the export boundary.

### Runtime ecosystem and configuration {#sec-model-serving-frameworknative-serving-da62}

Serving a model directly from the Python interpreter used to train it is the fastest path to a working endpoint, but under production load the interpreter itself becomes the bottleneck. Threads contend for the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), operators launch one by one without whole-graph fusion, and dynamic allocations fragment memory. Engine selection therefore starts with the binding system constraint rather than the training framework. When rapid iteration and full support for dynamic Python control flow or custom operators matter most, PyTorch and TensorFlow models can serve directly through their native runtimes. When interpreter overhead limits throughput, serialized graph formats such as `torch.export` and TensorFlow SavedModel (with TorchScript supporting legacy deployments) capture a static operator graph for ahead-of-time optimization and multi-threaded C++ execution. Framework-native runtimes prioritize developer flexibility and broad operator coverage, whereas specialized inference engines trade that generality for whole-graph rewrites and lower launch overhead.

#### General-purpose optimization {#sec-model-serving-generalpurpose-optimization-9ec2}

The development framework and deployment runtime need not be the same system, but they must exchange a representation both can interpret. The **ONNX**\index{ONNX!definition}\index{ONNX!cross-framework portability} format addresses this fragmentation by standardizing model exchange across runtimes [@bai2019onnx]. A pipeline can train an architecture in PyTorch, export the computation graph to an ONNX intermediate representation, and execute the serialized graph in ONNX Runtime or compile it for a target accelerator. In contrast, TensorFlow Lite relies on its own conversion path, translating TensorFlow SavedModels into FlatBuffers rather than routing through ONNX. Although standard interchange formats reduce manual model conversion between development and production environments, they do not eliminate compatibility testing, operator coverage gaps, or custom-kernel fallback overhead.

The exchange is hub-and-spoke\index{ONNX!hub-and-spoke interoperability} around the common ONNX intermediate representation (@fig-onnx). Training frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Caffe2, MXNet, and CNTK export inward to the shared representation, and ONNX Runtime and other target frameworks load the serialized computation graph outward without reimplementing model code.

::: {#fig-onnx fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Framework Interoperability**: The inward spokes represent exports into the shared ONNX format, while the outward spokes represent loads into compatible tools and runtimes; portability requires support on both sides of that boundary." fig-alt="Hub diagram with ONNX at center. Left side (export): PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Caffe2, MXNet, Microsoft CNTK with arrows pointing inward. Right side (load): ONNX Runtime plus the same six frameworks with arrows pointing outward."}

![](../07_frameworks/images/jpeg/onnx_new.jpg){width=66%}

:::

Interchange formats mitigate framework fragmentation, but an export boundary cannot salvage an architecture that violates the target's physical limits. Converting a graph to ONNX or an embedded runtime after development completes cannot resolve an excessive memory footprint, missing hardware operators, or unsupported dynamic control flow. Treating deployment as an afterthought guarantees costly rewrites, which is why hardware and runtime trade-offs need evaluating before the first line of model code is written.

When cross-hardware portability is the binding constraint, ONNX Runtime[^fn-onnx-runtime-serving] provides an intermediate, hardware-agnostic execution layer [@onnxruntime2024]. Models export to the ONNX format, after which ONNX Runtime applies target-independent graph optimizations and delegates subgraphs to hardware-specific execution providers. This architecture enables single-format deployment across CPUs, GPUs, and custom accelerator application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs).

Portability still demands profiling operator placement across execution boundaries. If an operation is unsupported by the preferred execution provider, placement depends on the configured provider order and available implementations. A CPU fallback can introduce host-accelerator transfers and synchronization that erode the expected latency advantage; if no provider supports the operation, execution may fail. Profiling must therefore verify provider assignment and operator coverage across the entire graph, not merely confirm that the exported artifact executes without errors.

[^fn-onnx-runtime-serving]: **ONNX Runtime**\index{ONNX Runtime!cross-platform serving}: Microsoft's inference engine applies graph optimizations such as constant folding, redundant-node elimination, and kernel fusion before handing subgraphs to execution providers. Performance relative to a tuned target-specific engine such as TensorRT depends on the workload, execution provider, and hardware.

#### Specialized inference engines {#sec-model-serving-specialized-inference-engines-475f}

When latency budgets or serving costs bind more tightly than portability, specialized engines such as TensorRT\index{Inference!engine, specialized} for NVIDIA GPUs and OpenVINO[^fn-openvino-cpu-inference] for Intel hardware optimize graphs specifically for target microarchitectures [@nvidia2024tensorrt; @openvinoDocs; @chen2018tvm]. Rather than maintaining portable abstractions, these compilers specialize kernels directly to the hardware's register files, cache hierarchies, and matrix execution units. A specialized engine such as TensorRT or TVM offers no advantage unless its backend supports the target and its conversion path supports the model [@nvidia2024tensorrt; @chen2018tvm], and ONNX reduces the exchange burden without proving either condition [@bai2019onnx].

[^fn-openvino-cpu-inference]: **OpenVINO (open visual inference and neural network optimization)**\index{OpenVINO!Intel inference}: An Intel-oriented inference toolkit that converts, optimizes, and runs models across Intel CPU, GPU, and NPU targets [@openvinoDocs]. Specializing for direct hardware execution departs from the portable execution guarantees of general-purpose frameworks, enabling the compiler to emit architecture-tuned vector instructions (such as AVX-512 or AMX) and exploit low-precision integer execution units. While speedups depend on the specific operator mix and target processor, this specialization can make CPU or edge serving economically viable for latency-sensitive models.

Layer fusion[^fn-layer-fusion-serving]\index{Layer fusion|see{Kernel fusion}}\index{Kernel fusion!serving compilers} is kernel fusion (also called operator fusion) applied when the engine is built. For the convolution $\to$ batch normalization $\to$ ReLU block, whose folding @sec-model-compression-operator-fusion-ac1d derives, the serving compiler performs the fold once, at engine build time, because batch normalization is a fixed affine transform once training ends. It absorbs the normalization into the convolution weights and bias, then fuses the ReLU into the same kernel, so the input feature map is read from HBM once and only the activated result is written back.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Kernel fusion, which merges adjacent operations so intermediates stay in registers and on-chip memory instead of round-tripping through HBM, is established in @sec-ml-frameworks-execution-strategy-matters-memory-wall-1ce8.
:::

[^fn-layer-fusion-serving]: **Layer fusion**\index{Kernel fusion!layer fusion}: The term parallels loop fusion in compiler optimization, where adjacent loops over the same array are combined into one pass to reduce memory traffic.

Kernel auto-tuning\index{Kernel auto-tuning!algorithm selection} benchmarks and selects the optimal algorithm for each operation on the target microarchitecture. A single 2D convolution can be evaluated through direct convolution, GEMM transformation (im2col), Winograd minimal filtering (efficient for small $3 \times 3$ filters), or Fast Fourier Transforms (efficient for large spatial filters), alongside dozens of tile-size variations. Because the winning strategy depends on filter dimensions, batch size, and the accelerator's register and shared memory capacity, the compiler benchmarks candidate implementations against target hardware and caches the lowest-latency kernel, trading ahead-of-time compilation time for predictable serving latency. Together with operator fusion, these optimizations produce substantial speedups over an untuned framework-native baseline, though they require explicit graph compilation and may restrict dynamic tensor dimensions.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: runtime-comparison-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RUNTIME COMPARISON
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "ResNet-50: Runtime Comparison"—specialized inference
# │          engines section
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the speedup spectrum across inference runtimes.
# │ Show: That removing per-operation overhead, not precision, gives most of the batch-one speedup.
# │ How: ResNetH100Profile per engine: issue cost, kernel count, weight bytes, per-image time.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, fmt_time, check

class RuntimeComparisonCalc:
    """ResNet-50 runtime ladder at batch one on the H100: each engine removes one term of the profile."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    P = ResNetH100Profile
    rt_pytorch_ms_value = P.eager_b1
    rt_torchscript_ms_value = P.torchscript_b1
    rt_onnx_ms_value = P.onnx_b1
    rt_trt_fp32_ms_value = P.trt_fp32_b1
    rt_trt_fp16_ms_value = P.trt_fp16_b1
    rt_trt_int8_ms_value = P.trt_int8_b1

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    rt_pytorch_speedup_value = 1.0
    rt_torchscript_speedup_value = (rt_pytorch_ms_value / rt_torchscript_ms_value).to("").magnitude
    rt_onnx_speedup_value = (rt_pytorch_ms_value / rt_onnx_ms_value).to("").magnitude
    rt_trt_fp32_speedup_value = (rt_pytorch_ms_value / rt_trt_fp32_ms_value).to("").magnitude
    rt_trt_fp16_speedup_value = (rt_pytorch_ms_value / rt_trt_fp16_ms_value).to("").magnitude
    rt_trt_int8_speedup_value = (rt_pytorch_ms_value / rt_trt_int8_ms_value).to("").magnitude
    int8_over_fp32_value = (rt_trt_fp32_ms_value / rt_trt_int8_ms_value).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(rt_trt_fp32_speedup_value > 5, "Prose: removing per-operation overhead gives most of the speedup.")
    check(int8_over_fp32_value < 1.5, "Prose: at batch one, precision adds little once overhead is gone.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    rt_pytorch_ms_str = fmt_time(rt_pytorch_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    rt_torchscript_ms_str = fmt_time(rt_torchscript_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    rt_onnx_ms_str = fmt_time(rt_onnx_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    rt_trt_fp32_ms_str = fmt_time(rt_trt_fp32_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    rt_trt_fp16_ms_str = fmt_time(rt_trt_fp16_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    rt_trt_int8_ms_str = fmt_time(rt_trt_int8_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    rt_pytorch_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(1, precision=0, commas=False)
    rt_torchscript_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(rt_torchscript_speedup_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
    rt_onnx_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(rt_onnx_speedup_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
    rt_trt_fp32_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(rt_trt_fp32_speedup_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
    rt_trt_fp16_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(rt_trt_fp16_speedup_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
    rt_trt_int8_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(rt_trt_int8_speedup_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
    int8_over_fp32_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(int8_over_fp32_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
```

::: {#exmp-model-serving-resnet-50-runtime-comparison .callout-example title="ResNet-50: Runtime comparison"}

@Tbl-model-serving-runtime-comparison applies the chapter's profile to each engine at batch one on the reference H100, changing one term at a time. The eager row is the reference profile. TorchScript runs the same kernels from a graph executor, removing the per-operation Python dispatch. ONNX Runtime also fuses each convolution with its normalization, activation, and residual add, cutting `{python} ResNetH100Profile.eager_kernels_str` kernels to `{python} ResNetH100Profile.fused_kernels_str`. TensorRT replays the whole fused pass as one captured graph and then varies only the number format.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
%\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

| **Runtime**         |                      **Latency**                       |                           **Speedup**                            | **Notes**                 |
|:--------------------|:------------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------|
| **PyTorch (eager)** |   `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_pytorch_ms_str`   |   `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_pytorch_speedup_mult_str`   | Reference profile         |
| **TorchScript**     | `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_torchscript_ms_str` | `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_torchscript_speedup_mult_str` | No per-op Python dispatch |
| **ONNX Runtime**    |    `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_onnx_ms_str`     |    `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_onnx_speedup_mult_str`     | Fused kernels             |
| **TensorRT FP32**   |  `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_fp32_ms_str`   |  `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_fp32_speedup_mult_str`   | One graph launch; TF32    |
| **TensorRT FP16**   |  `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_fp16_ms_str`   |  `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_fp16_speedup_mult_str`   | FP16 Tensor Cores         |
| **TensorRT INT8**   |  `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_int8_ms_str`   |  `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_int8_speedup_mult_str`   | Requires calibration      |

: **Inference runtime comparison**: Modeled batch-one latency and speedup for ResNet-50 on the reference H100 across PyTorch eager, TorchScript, ONNX Runtime, and TensorRT, from the chapter's serving profile. {#tbl-model-serving-runtime-comparison tbl-colwidths="[30,20,20,30]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

**Systems insight**: Removing per-operation overhead, not lowering precision, produces most of the batch-one speedup. TensorRT FP32 is already `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.rt_trt_fp32_speedup_mult_str` faster than eager execution, and INT8 adds only `{python} RuntimeComparisonCalc.int8_over_fp32_mult_str` over FP32, because once host overhead is gone the per-kernel floor dominates a single image. Precision pays at large batch, where per-image work dominates; INT8 also requires calibration data and NVIDIA-specific deployment.

:::

This optimization-compatibility trade-off governs engine selection. Higher specialization can improve hardware efficiency for supported operations and shapes but increases deployment complexity, restricts dynamic control flow, and may introduce numerical deviations from the training baseline. The engineering choice depends on latency budgets, operational constraints, and how frequently model architectures evolve.

Once an execution engine is selected, configuration tunes its resource allocation to the hardware envelope. For CPU inference, thread pool sizes must match physical core counts: too few threads leave execution units idle, while too many cause CPU cache thrashing, OS scheduling delays, and lock contention across non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domains. For accelerators, static memory preallocation reserves fixed-size activation workspaces during initialization, removing runtime memory allocations (`cudaMalloc`) and page-table faults from the latency-critical request path. Execution provider priority determines which hardware backend handles each operator subgraph, while graph optimization levels balance build times against constant folding and algebraic simplification. Production deployments must benchmark these configurations across full latency distributions (p50, p99) rather than relying on framework defaults.

### Precision selection for serving {#sec-model-serving-precision-selection-serving-55ba}

On the reference H100, Tensor Cores execute FP16, FP8, and INT8 matrix operations, and each halving of the bytes per value doubles the dense peak rate. For ResNet-50, moving from FP32 to INT8 multiplies large-batch throughput several times over while sacrificing less than 0.4 percentage points of top-1 accuracy. Numerical precision is therefore coupled directly to infrastructure economics. At the serving layer, precision engineering introduces operational constraints: calibration data fidelity, layer sensitivity under live inputs, and dynamic precision dispatch.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The quantization techniques this selection draws on, from numerical formats through calibration and quantization-aware training, are established in @sec-model-compression-quantization-precision-cd46.
:::

#### Precision-throughput relationship {#sec-model-serving-precisionthroughput-relationship-b503}

For memory-bandwidth-bound operations\index{Memory-bandwidth bound!precision impact}, reducing precision\index{Precision!throughput trade-off}\index{Quantization!serving precision} raises throughput by cutting the byte volume transferred across the memory bus. @Eq-precision-throughput gives the bandwidth-only upper bound from precision reduction:
$$
\frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{INT8}}}{\text{Throughput}_{\text{FP32}}} = \frac{32}{8} = 4\times \text{ (theoretical maximum)}
$$ {#eq-precision-throughput}

Actual speedup depends on the compute-to-memory ratio, operator mix, hardware instruction throughput, and matrix alignment, falling below the bandwidth-only bound whenever arithmetic throughput or memory alignment binds. Low-precision kernels achieve peak arithmetic efficiency only when matrix dimensions align with the accelerator's warp-level execution tiles (for example, multiples of 8 or 16 elements). When dimensions do not align with hardware tiles, libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN pad tensors or fall back to slower execution paths.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tensor Core tile architectures and their matrix-dimension alignment constraints are established in @sec-hardware-acceleration-tensor-cores-771f.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: precision-trade-off-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRECISION TRADEOFFS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "ResNet-50: Precision trade-offs on the H100"—precision-
# │          throughput relationship section
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the three-way trade-off between latency, memory, and accuracy.
# │ Show: That precision barely moves batch-one latency but multiplies large-batch throughput.
# │ How: Profile engines at batch one; FP32/FP16 ceilings modeled, INT8 measured by MLPerf.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import BYTES_FP32
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_pp, fmt_time, fmt_memory, fmt_rate

class PrecisionTradeoffCalc:
    """ResNet-50 precision trade-offs on the H100: batch-one latency, large-batch throughput, weights, accuracy."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    P = ResNetH100Profile
    pt_fp32_ms_value = P.trt_fp32_b1
    pt_fp16_ms_value = P.trt_fp16_b1
    pt_int8_ms_value = P.trt_int8_b1
    pt_fp32_tput = P.tf32_ceiling_img_s  # modeled, TF32 Tensor Cores at the sustained fraction
    pt_fp16_tput = P.eager_ceiling_img_s  # modeled, FP16 at the sustained fraction
    pt_int8_tput = P.int8_offline_img_s  # measured, MLPerf Inference v5.0 Offline
    pt_fp32_mem = P.resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    pt_fp16_mem = P.weights_fp16
    pt_int8_mem = P.weights_int8
    pt_fp32_acc_pct_value = 76.13  # scenario assumption: top-1 accuracy
    pt_fp16_acc_pct_value = 76.13  # scenario assumption: top-1 accuracy
    pt_int8_ptq_acc_pct_value = 75.80  # scenario assumption: top-1 accuracy after PTQ
    pt_int8_qat_acc_pct_value = 76.05  # scenario assumption: top-1 accuracy after QAT

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    pt_int8_b1_speedup_value = (pt_fp32_ms_value / pt_int8_ms_value).to("").magnitude
    pt_int8_tput_gain_value = pt_int8_tput / pt_fp32_tput
    pt_int8_acc_loss_value = pt_fp32_acc_pct_value - pt_int8_ptq_acc_pct_value
    pt_gpus_int8 = 10  # sizing example
    pt_gpus_fp32_equiv = round(pt_gpus_int8 * pt_int8_tput_gain_value)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pt_int8_b1_speedup_value < 1.5, "Prose: at batch one INT8 barely beats FP32.")
    check(pt_int8_tput_gain_value > 4, "Prose: at large batch INT8 sustains several times FP32's throughput.")
    check(round(pt_int8_acc_loss_value, 2) == 0.33, f"Expected 0.33pp accuracy loss, got {pt_int8_acc_loss_value}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    pt_fp32_ms_str = fmt_time(pt_fp32_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    pt_fp16_ms_str = fmt_time(pt_fp16_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    pt_int8_ms_str = fmt_time(pt_int8_ms_value, 'millisecond', precision=2, commas=False)
    pt_fp32_tput_str = fmt_rate(round(pt_fp32_tput, -2), 'img/s', precision=0, commas=True)
    pt_fp16_tput_str = fmt_rate(round(pt_fp16_tput, -2), 'img/s', precision=0, commas=True)
    pt_int8_tput_str = fmt_rate(round(pt_int8_tput, -2), 'img/s', precision=0, commas=True)
    pt_fp32_mem_mb_str = fmt_memory(pt_fp32_mem, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    pt_fp16_mem_mb_str = fmt_memory(pt_fp16_mem, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    pt_int8_mem_mb_str = fmt_memory(pt_int8_mem, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    pt_fp32_acc_str = fmt_percent(pt_fp32_acc_pct_value / 100, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
    pt_fp16_acc_str = fmt_percent(pt_fp16_acc_pct_value / 100, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
    pt_int8_ptq_acc_str = fmt_percent(pt_int8_ptq_acc_pct_value / 100, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
    pt_int8_qat_acc_str = fmt_percent(pt_int8_qat_acc_pct_value / 100, precision=2, commas=False, style='symbol')
    pt_int8_b1_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(pt_int8_b1_speedup_value, 1), precision=None, commas=False)
    pt_int8_tput_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(pt_int8_tput_gain_value), precision=0, commas=False)
    pt_int8_acc_loss_str = fmt_pp(pt_int8_acc_loss_value, precision=2)
    pt_gpus_int8_str = fmt(pt_gpus_int8, precision=0, commas=False)
    pt_gpus_fp32_equiv_str = fmt(pt_gpus_fp32_equiv, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#exmp-model-serving-resnet-50-precision-trade-offs-v100 .callout-example title="ResNet-50: Precision trade-offs on the H100"}

@Tbl-model-serving-precision-tradeoffs compares FP32, FP16, and two INT8 paths for ResNet-50 on the reference H100: batch-one latency for each TensorRT engine of the chapter's profile, throughput at large batch, weight bytes, and assumed accuracy:

| **Precision**  |               **Batch-1 Latency**               |             **Large-Batch Throughput**            |                     **Weights**                     |                     **Accuracy**                     | **Calibration**     |
|:---------------|:-----------------------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------:|:--------------------|
| **FP32**       | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp32_ms_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp32_tput_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp32_mem_mb_str` |   `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp32_acc_str`   | None                |
| **FP16**       | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp16_ms_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp16_tput_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp16_mem_mb_str` |   `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_fp16_acc_str`   | None                |
| **INT8 (PTQ)** | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_ms_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_tput_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_mem_mb_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_ptq_acc_str` | 1,000 samples       |
| **INT8 (QAT)** | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_ms_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_tput_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_mem_mb_str` | `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_qat_acc_str` | Additional training |

: **Precision trade-offs on the H100**: Modeled batch-one latency for each TensorRT engine of the chapter's profile; large-batch throughput modeled at the sustained fraction for FP32 (on TF32 Tensor Cores) and FP16, and measured by MLPerf Inference for INT8; weight bytes from the registry; assumed top-1 accuracy. {#tbl-model-serving-precision-tradeoffs tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,14,16,20]"}

**Systems insight**: At batch one, INT8 is only `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_b1_speedup_mult_str` faster than FP32, because the fixed per-kernel cost dominates a single image. At large batch it sustains about `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_tput_gain_mult_str` FP32's throughput and loses `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_int8_acc_loss_str` of accuracy with PTQ. QAT recovers most of that loss but requires retraining.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp8-serving-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FP8 AS THE DEFAULT SERVING PRECISION ON AN H100
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Paragraph after the ResNet-50 precision example in
# │          @sec-model-serving-precisionthroughput-relationship-b503.
# │
# │ Goal: Show that on the reference H100 an 8-bit float format doubles peak
# │       arithmetic and halves weight bytes relative to FP16.
# │ Show: FP16 and FP8 dense peaks; GPT-2 XL weight bytes and decode floor
# │       in each format.
# │ How: Registry H100 precision peaks and bandwidth; storage widths from the
# │      precision map (FP8 stores one byte per value).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, GB, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.core.units import resolve_precision, TFLOPs
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_memory, fmt_time, fmt_multiple

class Fp8Serving:
    """FP16 vs. FP8 peak arithmetic and GPT-2 XL decode floor on an H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2
    _, bytes_fp16 = resolve_precision("fp16")
    _, bytes_fp8 = resolve_precision("fp8")

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    peak_fp16 = h100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    peak_fp8 = h100.compute.precision_flops["fp8"]
    peak_ratio = (peak_fp8 / peak_fp16).to("").magnitude
    weights_fp16 = gpt2.size_in_bytes(bytes_fp16).to(GB)
    weights_fp8 = gpt2.size_in_bytes(bytes_fp8).to(GB)
    floor_fp16 = (weights_fp16 / h100.memory.bandwidth).to(millisecond)
    floor_fp8 = (weights_fp8 / h100.memory.bandwidth).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(peak_ratio - 2.0) < 0.05, f"FP8 peak should be about twice FP16 on an H100, got {peak_ratio:.2f}x.")
    check(abs((floor_fp16 / floor_fp8).to("").magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-6, "FP8 must halve the weight-read floor.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    peak_fp16_str = fmt_flop_rate(peak_fp16, unit=TFLOPs / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    peak_fp8_str = fmt_flop_rate(peak_fp8, unit=TFLOPs / second, precision=0, commas=True)
    peak_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(peak_ratio), precision=0, commas=False)
    weights_fp16_gb_str = fmt_memory(weights_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    weights_fp8_gb_str = fmt_memory(weights_fp8, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    floor_fp16_ms_str = fmt_time(floor_fp16, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    floor_fp8_ms_str = fmt_time(floor_fp8, unit="millisecond", precision=2, commas=False)
```

Integer formats are not the only 8-bit option. On the reference H100, an 8-bit floating-point format (FP8, whose E4M3 layout for weights and activations @sec-model-compression-quantization-precision-cd46 introduced) is the natural serving default for transformer workloads. The H100's dense FP8 peak of `{python} Fp8Serving.peak_fp8_str` is `{python} Fp8Serving.peak_ratio_mult_str` its FP16 peak of `{python} Fp8Serving.peak_fp16_str`, and each value occupies one byte instead of two. For the chapter's GPT-2 XL service, FP8 weights shrink from `{python} Fp8Serving.weights_fp16_gb_str` to `{python} Fp8Serving.weights_fp8_gb_str`, which lowers the bandwidth floor on a batch-one decode step from `{python} Fp8Serving.floor_fp16_ms_str` to `{python} Fp8Serving.floor_fp8_ms_str`. Because the format keeps a floating-point exponent, it tolerates the wide activation ranges of transformers better than INT8, though it still needs per-tensor scale factors and an accuracy check before deployment.

#### Precision selection constraints {#sec-model-serving-layer-sensitivity-6a31}

Quantizing every layer of a network to INT8 indiscriminately, or calibrating scale factors on daytime studio photos before serving nighttime camera feeds, can cost several percentage points of accuracy. Precision selection is constrained by layer sensitivity\index{Quantization!layer sensitivity}\index{Layer sensitivity!precision tolerance}, calibration data, and runtime policy. Not all layers tolerate reduced precision equally. The error bound of the uniform quantizer, half a quantization step inside the calibrated clipping range plus saturation error outside it (@sec-model-compression-quantization-precision-cd46, with the step from @eq-quant-scale), limits what each layer must absorb. Layer-level output or task error depends on activation distributions and downstream sensitivity, so it must be measured rather than inferred from a universal norm law. This mechanism explains why first convolutional and final classification layers are commonly retained at FP16, while intermediate layers tolerate INT8. Initial layers process low-dimensional raw inputs (such as 3 RGB channels) before representations expand into overcomplete feature spaces that can absorb quantization noise. Final classification layers, by contrast, produce raw logits where small numerical perturbations directly shift decision boundaries and alter top-$1$ predictions.

Post-training quantization\index{Post-training quantization!calibration} adds a data dependency. The calibration dataset\index{Calibration!dataset, representative traffic}\index{Calibration!INT8 quantization} determines the clipping thresholds $[\ClippingRangeLowerBound, \ClippingRangeUpperBound]$ and scale factors $\QuantizationScale$ used for INT8 conversion, requiring it to match the statistical profile of live serving traffic rather than arbitrary training or validation splits. A calibration-serving distribution mismatch causes excessive clipping or underflow, degrading end-to-end task accuracy, an operational pitfall analyzed in @sec-model-serving-fallacies-pitfalls-336b.

Production serving architectures can also turn precision\index{Precision!dynamic, adaptive quality} from a static compilation setting into a dynamic runtime policy. When request queues are shallow and the system operates with ample latency headroom against its service level objective (SLO), the engine can dispatch requests at FP16 to maximize task accuracy. During traffic spikes that threaten queue saturation, the engine can dynamically switch execution to INT8 to preserve latency bounds. Similarly, requests that yield low classification confidence under INT8 can be selectively re-evaluated at FP16, trading a small accuracy margin for lower latency when traffic spikes.

Precision selection carries direct infrastructure sizing consequences. Under the large-batch throughput gain of @tbl-model-serving-precision-tradeoffs, `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_gpus_int8_str` GPUs at INT8 offer the same aggregate saturated capacity as about `{python} PrecisionTradeoffCalc.pt_gpus_fp32_equiv_str` GPUs at FP32. Equal capacity does not establish equal queueing latency; service-time distributions, batching policy, and failure reserve must still satisfy the same SLO. Precision engineering is therefore an infrastructure sizing discipline, directly coupling numerical representation to cluster capital expense and energy consumption. Yet configuring the runtime and numerical bit width addresses only the model level; achieving low-latency serving in production requires optimizing the host-to-device boundaries within the physical server node itself.

## Node-Level Optimization {#sec-model-serving-nodelevel-optimization-3d9d}

The reference ResNet-50 request spends `{python} LatencyTableCalc.l_inf_ms_str` in the forward pass and `{python} LatencyTableCalc.l_total_ms_str` end to end. Once a compiled engine shrinks the forward pass to the modeled `{python} LatencyBudgetCalc.tensorrt_inference_ms_str`, preprocessing alone accounts for `{python} LatencyBudgetCalc.tensorrt_preprocess_pct_str` of what remains. An isolated model benchmark hides exactly these costs, because they sit on the host: JPEG decoding on CPU cores, copies across the PCIe bus, and the driver work that launches each kernel.

Runtime selection and precision tuning operate at the model level, determining what computation runs and what numerical format it uses. Between the model graph and the silicon, however, lies an execution layer encompassing graph compilation, bus transfers, and CPU-accelerator coordination. Node-level optimization targets this complete end-to-end request path on concrete hardware, eliminating overhead between the network socket and accelerator execution units across four primary physical boundaries:

- **Graph-to-kernel boundary**: Translating computation graphs\index{Graph compilation!optimization} into numerous fine-grained kernel launches incurs driver serialization overhead and forces intermediate tensors through device HBM. Graph compilers fuse adjacent operations into composite kernels that preserve intermediate activations in on-chip SRAM or register files.
- **Host-accelerator boundary**: Accelerators sit idle when the host processor fails to enqueue work ahead of execution. Unpipelined copies across host-device interconnects (such as PCIe) and blocking synchronization calls stall accelerator compute pipelines.
- **CPU execution boundary**: Host preprocessing pipelines and CPU-based inference degrade when executed through interpreted scalar code rather than vectorized single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) instruction units and NUMA-local memory allocations, and when operating-system noise preempts the threads that feed the accelerator.
- **Storage and deserialization boundary**: Initializing serving replicas requires streaming weight tensors from persistent storage into host memory. Formats requiring recursive object deserialization bottleneck CPU execution, creating cold-start latency spikes that impede autoscaling. This boundary governs how quickly a replica starts rather than how fast it serves, so @sec-model-serving-loading-strategies-eb38 develops it with the rest of model loading.

Each boundary represents a distinct physical constraint where execution stalls on memory bandwidth, bus transit, or control overhead rather than peak arithmetic throughput. The subsections that follow cross these boundaries from the accelerator outward—from runtime graph compilation and host-to-accelerator execution pipelines to CPU locality, model loading, and multi-model memory sharing.

### Runtime graph compilation {#sec-model-serving-runtime-graph-compilation-7a7e}

Crossing the first of those boundaries—the graph-to-kernel interface—without compilation leaves the host CPU submitting tiny kernels one operator at a time across a 32-layer transformer or 50-layer convnet, often spending more time in the driver than the GPU spends on the math. Specialized inference engines (@sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef) beat eager framework baselines because serving workloads run fixed operator graphs over bounded input shapes. When the operator sequence and tensor dimensions are known before live traffic arrives, compilers move graph optimization from the per-request critical path to offline deployment preparation.

The whole-graph rewrites that make this shift pay are the ones the specialized engines apply at build time. Kernel fusion\index{Kernel fusion!graph compilation} and the batch-normalization fold of @sec-model-serving-specialized-inference-engines-475f, the canonical case of compile-time constant folding\index{Constant folding!compile-time optimization}\index{Optimization!compile-time, constant folding}, remove launches and intermediate-memory traffic from every request. Static memory planning\index{Memory planning!tensor allocation} (@sec-hardware-acceleration-memory-planning-fb9f) reuses one preallocated arena for tensors whose lifetimes do not overlap, which keeps allocator calls off the request path. In a serving trace, repeated launch overhead and intermediate-memory traffic point to missing fusion, and allocation stalls on the request path point to a missing memory plan.

Beyond memory planning and kernel fusion, static execution paths can use CUDA Graphs\index{CUDA graphs!kernel launch elimination}\index{Kernel launch latency!driver overhead reduction}, the replay of a captured sequence of kernel launches that @sec-ml-frameworks-hybrid-approaches-jit-compilation-8954 developed. Each eager submission pays the 5–20 $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ of host launch work quantified in @sec-model-serving-batching-helps-f1dc, and total submission cost depends on the executed kernel count, not the number of layers. A decode step launching 8 to 10 sub-kernels across each of 32 transformer layers can accumulate several milliseconds of host submission work, longer than the accelerator needs for the tensor math at small batch sizes. Serving systems therefore capture the graph during warmup, once per supported batch size because replay requires static shapes and fixed buffer addresses. They dispatch it during live inference with a single driver invocation (illustratively $\sim 5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$, depending on the graph, driver, and hardware). Replay removes repeated host submission work without eliminating device execution costs.

::: {#psp-model-serving-jit-vs-aot-compilation .callout-perspective title="Compilation timing trade-off"}

Just-in-time compilation\index{JIT compilation!runtime optimization} defers graph optimization until the runtime engine observes concrete input shapes and execution paths. This runtime visibility enables aggressive kernel specialization for dynamic control flow and variable sequence lengths, but it injects compilation overhead directly into the serving path, generating multi-second latency spikes on early requests.

Ahead-of-time compilation\index{Ahead-of-time compilation!predeployment} executes graph analysis, kernel fusion, and hardware-specific auto-tuning prior to deployment. Pre-building removes the covered compilation work from the request path, but weights, device contexts, allocations, and representative execution paths still require loading and warmup. The compiled engine remains constrained to its supported shape profiles and may require padding or multi-profile compilation to accommodate dynamic input sizes.

:::

### Deterministic latency and resource isolation {#sec-model-serving-deterministic-latency-resource-isolation-4d1c}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/model_serving_blast_radius.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal rows, each holding the same total length of blue work, under the label same pass. The top row is unbroken. The second row is split by one red gap and the third by two red gaps, so each row ends further right. A dashed gray line marks where the unbroken row ends, and a red bracket labeled jitter spans from that line to the end of the longest row."}

*Noisy neighbors stretch identical forward passes unevenly, widening the tail.*
:::

Compilation fixes what the accelerator executes; it does not control how steadily the host feeds it. The server shares its host with other work. On a single host, the operating system multiplexes hardware across background telemetry daemons, logging agents, and kernel worker threads. When these unisolated processes contend for execution resources, they intermittently preempt the inference pipeline. These noisy neighbors are a primary source of **latency jitter**\index{Latency jitter!resource contention}, where the physical time required to execute identical forward passes fluctuates unpredictably. This contention inflates 99th percentile (p99) tail latency even when average hardware utilization remains low. Resource contention thus widens tail latency through service-time variance, a physical degradation distinct from the queuing-delay accumulation along the saturation knee plotted in @fig-tail-latency-explosion.

Keeping latency predictable\index{Latency!deterministic}\index{Resource isolation!serving} requires isolating the serving process from the operating system's default time-sharing scheduler. Serving systems such as Clockwork demonstrate that deep neural network (DNN) inference execution times can be predictable down to sub-millisecond tolerances under their controlled workload and hardware conditions [@gujarati2020]. CPU affinity (thread pinning)\index{CPU affinity!latency reduction} establishes the baseline compute boundary by binding inference worker threads to designated physical cores. Without pinning, the OS scheduler periodically migrates threads between cores, losing access to warm private L1 and L2 cache contents and requiring lines to be refetched from shared L3 cache or DRAM. On multi-socket architectures, thread migration across NUMA boundaries is even more penalizing. Accesses to memory left on the previous socket cross inter-socket interconnects, adding tens of nanoseconds of latency per transaction. Pinning threads to specific cores and binding their memory allocations to local NUMA nodes reduces migration-related cache misses and remote-socket memory traffic.

Even with pinned CPU cores, memory access latency remains vulnerable to the virtual memory subsystem. Under host memory pressure, the kernel can page inactive address ranges out to disk. When the CPU touches a paged-out address, execution can stall for milliseconds while the page returns to DRAM. Host buffers used for PCIe DMA also need resident, registered backing pages during the transfer. Memory locking (`mlock`)\index{Memory!locking, mlock} instructs the kernel to pin specified virtual address ranges into physical host RAM, preventing page eviction for host-resident weights, input staging buffers, and offloaded key-value (KV) cache blocks. This removes eviction-related page faults at the cost of host memory flexibility; locked pages remain resident until unlocked, while cache misses and memory contention can still delay access. Because `mlock` operates strictly on host page tables, it does not apply to accelerator HBM, which is allocated directly by the accelerator driver.

Beyond scheduled processes, asynchronous hardware interrupts introduce another source of sub-millisecond preemption. When a network interface card (NIC) receives packet bursts, it triggers hardware interrupt requests (IRQs) that force the handling CPU core to immediately suspend user-space execution and process kernel interrupt handlers. If the OS routes these interrupts to cores running the inference engine's submission loop, the CPU pauses command dispatch to the accelerator. Because GPUs process short inference layers in microseconds, even brief CPU submission stalls drain the accelerator's hardware command ring buffer, causing pipeline bubbles where compute units sit idle waiting for the next kernel descriptor. Interrupt shielding\index{Interrupt shielding!latency isolation} restricts IRQ affinities to dedicated housekeeping cores, reducing preemption of the GPU dispatch thread by those device interrupts.

Isolating physical cores, locking host memory, and shielding interrupt lines reduce specific sources of operating system noise, though the resulting service-time distribution still needs measurement under the intended load. Thus far, isolation has treated the host as a predictable partner that feeds a discrete accelerator; when deployment constraints or workload profiles dispense with the accelerator altogether, the host CPU becomes the executor itself.

### CPU inference optimization {#sec-model-serving-cpu-inference-optimization-ae86}

For a small fraud-detection or ranking model evaluated at batch size one, copying a single request across PCIe and launching GPU kernels through the driver can take longer than running the forward pass directly on the host processor. Deploying inference on CPUs\index{CPU!inference optimization} therefore remains practical for lightweight models, sparse or bursty request streams that cannot saturate an accelerator, and services where host-to-device transfer time exceeds the math time. Yet an untuned Python CPU path leaves most of the processor's silicon idle. Modern server CPUs[^fn-simd-cpu-serving]\index{SIMD!CPU vectorization} (such as Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC) include wide SIMD vector registers and matrix units (AVX-512 and AMX), which specialized runtimes such as OpenVINO target by tiling matrix operations across L1/L2 caches and emitting packed fused multiply-add (FMA) instructions [@openvinoDocs].

[^fn-simd-cpu-serving]: **SIMD**\index{SIMD!CPU inference}: From Michael Flynn's 1966 taxonomy of computer architectures, SIMD enables one instruction to operate on multiple data elements simultaneously. Intel's AVX-512 can process sixteen FP32 values in a 512-bit vector, while AMX adds matrix tile operations. The attainable fraction of peak depends on data type, matrix shape, memory behavior, and implementation, but optimized vector kernels provide multiple-fold speedups over scalar execution.

The NUMA\index{NUMA!memory locality}\index{NUMA!inference latency} boundaries that thread pinning respects matter more when the CPU itself runs the model. Memory controllers are physically distributed across CPU sockets and linked by coherent interconnects (such as Intel UPI or AMD Infinity Fabric). Accessing memory attached to a remote socket incurs substantially higher latency and lower bandwidth than local channel access. An inference server must maintain NUMA awareness. Worker threads\index{Thread pinning!CPU affinity} must be pinned to dedicated physical cores, and the weight tensors and request buffers those threads touch must reside in memory nodes local to that socket. Because model weights, at hundreds of megabytes to tens of gigabytes, routinely exceed per-socket L3 cache capacities, every forward pass streams weights from main RAM. Mismatched socket allocations force continuous weight streaming across the slower inter-socket interconnect, creating severe tail-latency degradation.

For lightweight models evaluated at batch size one, a CPU frequently outperforms a discrete GPU\index{Batching!batch, small, CPU advantage}. When an accelerator processes an isolated request, the fixed overhead of transferring inputs across the host PCIe bus (several microseconds), driver queue serialization, and kernel launch overhead (5–20 $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ per kernel) can easily surpass the arithmetic execution time. The CPU processes the request directly in local cache without bus transfers or driver queue delays. Determining the operational crossover requires empirical measurement across model architecture, arithmetic intensity, batch size, and latency constraints.

### Profiling the serving node {#sec-model-serving-profiling-serving-node-1e99}

Finding that crossover—or diagnosing why an accelerator-backed node misses its p99 target while average GPU utilization sits below 30 percent—requires inspecting where each request actually waits across the host and device. The top-down profiling method of @sec-model-training-identifying-bottlenecks-f57f applies unchanged to a serving node, where the objective is useful throughput that meets the latency SLO. The duty-cycle metric defined in @eq-system-efficiency helps locate idle intervals, but active time alone does not measure arithmetic efficiency or prove adequate queueing headroom. Timeline profilers\index{Timeline profiling!serving optimization}, such as PyTorch Profiler\index{Framework profiler!timeline analysis} and NVIDIA Nsight Systems (`nsys`)\index{GPU profiler!timeline analysis}, record concurrent CPU threads, OS runtime calls, memory transfers, and GPU hardware queues along a synchronized timeline.

Serving traces show three recurring signatures:

- **Idle compute bubbles**: White space on the GPU execution track indicates hardware starvation. Compute warps idle while waiting for the host CPU to complete request preprocessing (e.g., tokenization or image decoding), page faults during on-demand weight paging, or blocking inter-thread synchronization.
- **Kernel launch fragmentation**: A sequence of micro-kernels, each executing in under 5–10 $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$, suggests launch overhead as a candidate. Host launch timing and gaps between device kernels reveal whether submission starves the GPU; if so, graph capture or legal fusion may help.
- **Interconnect transfer stalls**: Synchronous `MemcpyHtoD` blocks on the primary CUDA stream indicate unpipelined host-to-device data movement. Overcoming this stall requires allocating page-locked (pinned) host memory and executing asynchronous transfers on dedicated copy streams to overlap bus transit with concurrent accelerator execution on preceding requests.

::: {#exmp-model-serving-profiling-loop .callout-example title="The profiling loop"}

**Scenario**: An inference serving node reports high p99 tail latency despite low average GPU compute utilization.

**Diagnosis**: Timeline profiling (Nsight Systems/PyTorch Profiler) reveals large idle gaps between tiny GPU kernels caused by CPU host-side preprocessing bottlenecks and kernel launch overhead.

**Systems lesson**: Serving node optimization requires empirical timeline profiling. Iteratively identifying trace bottlenecks (kernel launch overhead, host-device copy stalls) guides targeted optimizations like kernel fusion and pinned memory.

:::

@Tbl-optimization-impact summarizes representative node-level optimization techniques alongside their primary target metrics and engineering costs. The table serves as a decision matrix rather than an exhaustive checklist. Engineering effort should be directed exclusively to the row that addresses the binding bottleneck identified on the measured execution trace.

| **Technique**         | **Target Metric**    | **Illustrative Gain** | **Implement. Cost** | **Best For**           |
|:----------------------|:---------------------|:---------------------:|:--------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Kernel Fusion**     | Latency & Throughput |      2–5$\times$      | Medium (Compiler)   | Memory-bound layers    |
| **INT8 Quantization** | Throughput           |      3–4$\times$      | High (Calibration)  | Inference-heavy nodes  |
| **Graph Compilation** | Latency              |     1.5–3$\times$     | Low (One-line)      | Static graph models    |
| **Zero-Copy Loading** | Startup Time         |     10–50$\times$     | Low (File format)   | Autoscaling/Cold Start |
| **CPU Pinning**       | Tail Latency (p99)   |    20–50% reduction   | Low (Config)        | Latency-critical apps  |

: **Node-Level Optimization Impact**: Illustrative ranges for matching techniques to measured bottlenecks. Realized gains and implementation cost depend on the model, runtime, hardware, and workload. {#tbl-optimization-impact tbl-colwidths="[18,22,17,20,23]"}

This diagnostic hierarchy ensures engineering resources address structural bottlenecks along the entire request path rather than applying isolated micro-optimizations. A four-level audit checkpoint structures this prioritization from external service boundaries down to device kernels.

::: {#chk-model-serving-optimization-hierarchy .callout-checkpoint title="The optimization hierarchy"}

Optimizing inference follows the request path from the outside in across four structural levels:

- [ ] **System budget**: Partition the end-to-end latency budget between network transit, host application processing, queueing delay, and kernel execution using distributed tracing tools to verify compliance.
- [ ] **Application level**: Determine whether the arrival stream and latency budget permit batching, and test whether the gain in service capacity outweighs formation and resource-queue waiting.
- [ ] **Model level**: If dispatch or operator placement binds the request path, evaluate a compatible compiled engine or graph configuration and recheck quality across supported input shapes.
- [ ] **Kernel level**: Where intermediate traffic or launch overhead is measured, assess legal fusion candidates and verify their numerical behavior and end-to-end benefit.

:::

A node tuned this way runs each request near its physical limit, but only once it is running. The compiled engine that makes the steady state fast took tens of seconds to build, its weights must cross storage, host memory, and the PCIe bus before the first request arrives, and its preprocessing must match what training used. How a replica reaches that steady state, and whether it computes what training computed once there, decides whether the fast node is also a correct and available one.

## Model Loading and Versioning {#sec-model-serving-model-lifecycle-management-ff2e}

In a representative deployment, a newly provisioned replica needs 35 seconds before it can answer its first request, most of them spent compiling a TensorRT engine, while a subtle PIL-to-OpenCV preprocessing discrepancy silently costs five percentage points of classification accuracy. Every optimization so far assumed a replica that is already running and that computes the function training produced; both assumptions fail at the edges of a replica's life. Cold start delays the moment a new replica becomes useful, so it is controlled by how weights are loaded, cached, and shared across the models and versions that occupy one machine. Skew corrupts every prediction a correctly running replica makes, so it is prevented by keeping training and serving transformations identical; serving is where its symptom appears. The path below follows a replica from storage to a warmed engine, then to the several models and versions one machine may host, and ends with that symptom.

### Cold start and initialization dynamics {#sec-model-serving-model-loading-initialization-cc5a}

When an autoscaler spins up a new serving container during a traffic surge, that replica cannot answer a single request until its weights are loaded into memory, its execution graph is compiled, and its device buffers are initialized [@romero2021infaas]. This startup delay, known as cold start\index{Cold start!scaling events}, governs how quickly a service recovers from node failures or scales out into a spike.

::: {#dfn-model-serving-cold-start .callout-definition title="Cold start"}

***Cold start***\index{Cold start!definition} is the initialization latency incurred when starting a new model replica.

1.  **Significance**: It represents the fixed startup cost of loading weights, compiling graphs, and allocating buffers, which can take seconds or minutes and block elastic scaling during traffic bursts.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike inference latency $(\InferenceLatency)$, which is a per-request cost, cold start is an initialization cost paid when a replica or model instance is created, including deployment, scale-out, recovery, and on-demand model loading.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that cold start is "just loading weights." In reality, it includes graph compilation and memory allocation, which can often take longer than the bandwidth-limited data transfer itself $(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)$.

:::

Total cold-start latency compounds across four physical operations along the initialization path\index{Cold start!anatomy}. Weight loading\index{Weight loading!cold start} streams serialized parameters from persistent storage across the network or host I/O subsystem into host memory and then across the PCIe bus into GPU HBM. Graph compilation\index{Graph Compilation!JIT overhead} then lowers the framework computational graph into device-specific machine code by fusing operators and auto-tuning matrix multiplication kernels for the target accelerator. Once the compiled graph is ready, memory allocation reserves device arenas for activation scratchpads and intermediate buffers. Warmup\index{Warmup!cache population}[^fn-warmup-cold-start] execution then runs synthetic inferences to populate kernel caches, prime framework memory allocators, and complete any remaining lazy initialization before live traffic arrives.

[^fn-warmup-cold-start]: **Warmup**\index{Warmup!cold start mitigation}: Borrowed from just-in-time (JIT) compilation, where initial executions compile hot paths into optimized machine code; for ML serving, warmup inferences trigger CUDA kernel compilation, cuDNN algorithm auto-tuning, and memory pool allocation that frameworks defer until first use.

Establishing a CUDA context\index{CUDA!context, initialization overhead} is the first fixed cost on the device initialization timeline. Before launching any GPU kernel or allocating device memory, the runtime must instantiate a driver-level context: an internal control structure that manages virtual address spaces, loaded kernel binaries, and hardware event queues. Creating this context requires synchronous communication with the kernel-mode driver and allocates tens to hundreds of megabytes of device memory for bookkeeping. The 0.3–0.5 s range in @tbl-model-serving-resnet-coldstart reflects a typical data center environment. While CUDA lazy loading defers kernel module loading to shorten this initial pause, it merely defers that latency penalty to the first executed inference [@nvidiaCudaLazyLoading].

In multi-process serving deployments where multiple worker processes share a single accelerator, replicating individual CUDA contexts wastes both memory capacity and initialization time. CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS)\index{CUDA MPS!context sharing} coordinates concurrent work from multiple client processes, reducing scheduling overhead when individual processes underuse the device [@nvidiaCudaMps]. Its isolation behavior depends on the architecture. Pre-Volta clients shared a GPU address space; Volta clients retain separate GPU address spaces and contexts while their kernels can execute concurrently. Separate address spaces do not provide hard fault containment. A fatal GPU fault can affect other clients sharing the affected GPU, so the serving design must budget for correlated replica failures.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cold-start-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COLD START TIMELINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "ResNet-50: Cold Start Timeline"
# │
# │ Goal: Decompose the cold start latency of serverless inference.
# │ Show: That precompiling models reduces cold start from ~35 s to ~1.5 s.
# │ How: Sum phase durations for data transfer, CUDA initialization, and model loading.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_time, fmt_time_range, check

class ColdStartCalc:
    """Decomposes cold start latency showing precompiled TensorRT reduces startup from ~35 s to ~1.5 s."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    cs_ssd_value = 0.5 * second  # scenario assumption: weight loading from SSD
    cs_s3_value = 4.0 * second  # scenario assumption: weight loading from S3
    cs_cuda_value = 0.4 * second  # scenario assumption: CUDA context initialization
    cs_compile_value = 30.0 * second  # scenario assumption: TensorRT compilation
    cs_warmup_value = 0.2 * second  # scenario assumption: warmup inferences
    cs_runtime_overhead_value = 0.4 * second  # scenario assumption: runtime overhead

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    cs_local_total_value = cs_ssd_value + cs_cuda_value + cs_warmup_value + cs_runtime_overhead_value
    cs_cloud_total_value = cs_s3_value + cs_cuda_value + cs_compile_value + cs_warmup_value + cs_runtime_overhead_value

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(cs_local_total_value == 1.5 * second, f"Expected 1.5s local cold start, got {cs_local_total_value}")
    check(cs_cloud_total_value == 35.0 * second, f"Expected 35.0s cloud cold start, got {cs_cloud_total_value}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    cs_local_s_str = fmt_time(cs_local_total_value, 'second', precision=1, commas=False, approx=True)
    cs_cloud_s_str = fmt_time(cs_cloud_total_value, 'second', precision=0, commas=False, approx=True)
    cs_ssd_s_str = fmt_time(cs_ssd_value, 'second', precision=1, commas=False)
    cs_s3_str = fmt_time_range(3 * second, 5 * second, "second", precision=0, commas=False)
    cs_cuda_str = fmt_time_range(0.3 * second, 0.5 * second, "second", precision=1, commas=False)
    cs_compile_str = fmt_time_range(15 * second, 30 * second, "second", precision=0, commas=False)
    cs_warmup_s_str = fmt_time(cs_warmup_value, 'second', precision=1, commas=False)
    cs_runtime_overhead_s_str = fmt_time(cs_runtime_overhead_value, 'second', precision=1, commas=False)
```

::: {#exmp-model-serving-resnet-50-cold-start-timeline .callout-example title="ResNet-50: Cold start timeline"}

@Tbl-model-serving-resnet-coldstart traces the per-phase duration of a ResNet-50 cold start:

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}
```

| **Phase**                       |                    **Duration**                    | **Notes**                                           |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Weight loading (SSD)**        |       `{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_ssd_s_str`        | 98 MB FP32 weights from local storage               |
| **Weight loading (S3)**         |         `{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_s3_str`         | Network latency dominates for cloud storage         |
| **CUDA context**                |        `{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_cuda_str`        | GPU driver initialization and memory setup          |
| **TensorRT compilation**        |      `{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_compile_str`       | Converts PyTorch model to optimized engine          |
| **Warmup (10 inferences)**      |      `{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_warmup_s_str`      | Triggers remaining lazy initialization              |
| **Runtime overhead**            | `{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_runtime_overhead_s_str` | Process startup, framework hooks, and runtime setup |
| **Total (local, optimized)**    |    **`{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_local_s_str`**     | With precompiled TensorRT engine, warm container    |
| **Total (cloud, first deploy)** |    **`{python} ColdStartCalc.cs_cloud_s_str`**     | Including compilation from cold state               |

: **ResNet-50 cold start timeline**: Illustrative per-phase durations for weight loading, CUDA context creation, TensorRT compilation, and warmup, with totals for the optimized local case and the first-deploy cloud case showing where the dominant cost lives. {#tbl-model-serving-resnet-coldstart tbl-colwidths="[30,20,50]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
\vspace{-1.5ex}
```
**Systems insight**: Precompiling models and storing the optimized engine eliminates the 30-second compilation phase on subsequent deployments.

:::

Without warmup, the first live request absorbs deferred JIT compilation, driver memory allocation, and kernel launch overhead. A request whose steady-state forward pass takes `{python} ResNetH100Profile.eager_b1_ms_str` can stall for hundreds of milliseconds during an unmitigated cold start, violating strict SLOs. Controlling this initialization overhead requires systematic selection among storage, memory, and runtime loading strategies.

### Loading strategies and serialization formats {#sec-model-serving-loading-strategies-eb38}

Once precompilation removes the 30-second compiler step from @tbl-model-serving-resnet-coldstart, weight loading becomes the largest remaining term in the startup budget, and how the server schedules that read trades cold-start duration against first-request latency and memory footprint. The simplest approach, full loading\index{Model loading!full loading}, reads the entire model into memory before the server marks itself ready. This maximizes steady-state inference speed because all weights are resident in memory, but it stretches cold-start time and restricts model size to available memory. A second strategy, lazy initialization\index{Initialization!lazy, deferred compilation}, defers compilation and allocation until first use. This minimizes startup time but shifts latency to the first request, so production systems often combine lazy initialization with synthetic warmup requests to trigger initialization before real traffic arrives.

Autoscaling systems operate as closed-loop controllers that provision or deprovision serving replicas in response to traffic demand. During demand surges, cold-start latency governs how rapidly new replicas become ready to serve traffic. For multi-gigabyte models, cold-start duration is heavily dominated by streaming serialized model weights from persistent storage into host memory. The architectural choice of serialization format determines whether this stage is bounded by storage read bandwidth or by CPU parsing overhead.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: safetensors-loading-speed-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SAFETENSORS LOADING SPEED
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @exmp-model-serving-loading-speed-safetensors-vs-pickle and
# │          [^fn-safetensors-zerocopy-loading] in Node-Level Optimization.
# │
# │ Goal: Keep the checkpoint-size, load-time, and storage-bandwidth values in the
# │       loading-speed example traceable and consistently formatted.
# │ Show: Pickle vs. Safetensors load times for Stable Diffusion v1.5.
# │ How: Use the MLSysIM Stable Diffusion v1.5 model entry, the reusable
# │      cold-start loading scenario, and the Gen3 NVMe storage registry to
# │      compute the speedup.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class SafetensorsLoadingSpeed:
    """Loading-speed comparison for Pickle vs. Safetensors model weights."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.GenerativeVision.StableDiffusion_v1_5
    loading_scenario = ReferenceStats.ModelLoading
    checkpoint_size = loading_scenario.StableDiffusionV15CheckpointSize
    pickle_load = loading_scenario.StableDiffusionV15PickleLoadTime
    safetensors_load = loading_scenario.StableDiffusionV15SafetensorsLoadTime
    nvme_bw = Systems.Storage.LocalNvmeGen3.bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    load_speedup = pickle_load / safetensors_load

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(safetensors_load < pickle_load, "Safetensors example should load faster than Pickle.")
    check(
        safetensors_load >= checkpoint_size / nvme_bw * 0.9,
        "Safetensors load time should respect NVMe bandwidth for the checkpoint size.",
    )
    check(load_speedup.to("").magnitude > 1, "Loading speedup must exceed 1x.")
    check(
        checkpoint_size >= model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16),
        "Serialized checkpoint should be at least as large as raw FP16 model weights.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    checkpoint_size_gb_str = fmt_memory(checkpoint_size, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    pickle_load_s_str = fmt_time(pickle_load, unit=second, precision=0, commas=False)
    safetensors_load_s_str = fmt_time(safetensors_load, unit=second, precision=1, commas=False)
    nvme_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvme_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    load_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(load_speedup, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Legacy PyTorch checkpoints loaded via `torch.load()` package weights within a zip archive containing pickle-encoded object metadata\index{Pickle!loading overhead}. Deserializing a pickle file forces the CPU to interpret a stream of serialization opcodes sequentially, allocating individual Python objects (dictionaries, metadata wrappers, and tensor headers) and potentially copying tensor bytes into newly allocated memory. Restricted loading modes reduce arbitrary code execution risks, while memory-mapped options can avoid some eager copies. Whether parsing or storage dominates depends on the checkpoint, loading path, and hardware.

A tensor-oriented format[^fn-safetensors-zerocopy-loading] bypasses interpreter-driven object construction. Safetensors\index{Safetensors!zero-copy loading} organizes checkpoints with a lightweight header containing tensor metadata followed by contiguous, uncompressed tensor byte buffers aligned to memory boundaries. Because the on-disk binary layout mirrors the in-memory array layout, the runtime can use memory mapping\index{Memory mapping!on-demand model loading}\index{mmap!model loading} (`mmap(2)`), which maps file blocks directly into the process's virtual address space. Virtual memory pages fault into host RAM on access or are prefetched sequentially by the operating system, reducing Python object reconstruction and avoiding eager user-space tensor copies on the mapped path. Mapping shortens apparent startup, but a dense model eventually touches nearly all of its weights, so deferred page faults can move loading latency into early requests. The benefit is greater for sparsely accessed components or model repositories that load subsets on demand; latency-sensitive services still prefault or warm the pages needed on the request path. On systems with discrete accelerators, transferring these tensors across PCIe or NVLink is still required before computation begins, so memory-mapped host loading reduces CPU reconstruction costs without eliminating page faults, storage reads, or device initialization.

[^fn-safetensors-zerocopy-loading]: **Safetensors**\index{Safetensors!secure model loading}: The name emphasizes safety: unlike unrestricted pickle deserialization, the format does not encode executable Python objects [@huggingface_safetensors]. It stores tensors as contiguous raw bytes with a small header and supports memory-mapped loading. In the local benchmark example, that path is `{python} SafetensorsLoadingSpeed.load_speedup_mult_str` faster than the compared PyTorch checkpoint path; the result is workload- and storage-specific and does not include transfer to a discrete accelerator.

::: {#exmp-model-serving-loading-speed-safetensors-vs-pickle .callout-example title="Loading speed: Safetensors vs. Pickle"}

**Scenario**: A serverless inference replica loads a `{python} SafetensorsLoadingSpeed.checkpoint_size_gb_str` model checkpoint during cold-start scaling events.

**Diagnosis**: PyTorch `torch.load()` (Pickle) requires CPU object reconstruction, taking `{python} SafetensorsLoadingSpeed.pickle_load_s_str` to initialize. Safetensors memory-mapping bypasses CPU parsing, loading weights in `{python} SafetensorsLoadingSpeed.safetensors_load_s_str` (`{python} SafetensorsLoadingSpeed.load_speedup_mult_str` faster).

**Systems lesson**: Tensor-oriented, memory-mapped formats can reduce CPU reconstruction and eager-copy overhead during cold start. Storage throughput, page faults, runtime initialization, and accelerator transfer still remain in the scale-out budget.

:::

### Model caching infrastructure {#sec-model-serving-model-caching-infrastructure-4f1a}

Production systems also cache model weights at the infrastructure level to shorten cold start, and the right cache follows how often the model changes.
