Embedding the weights in the container image\index{Model caching!container embedding} yields a single deployment artifact with no network fetch at startup, but images of 10–50 GB slow every container pull, so the approach suits models that rarely update. A shared filesystem of versioned weights lets many replicas read one copy without rebuilding images, at the price of network latency in every cold start and a new availability dependency. It still requires an explicit, atomic version switch so that files never change underneath a live replica. Node-local SSD caching\index{SSD cache!model loading} prepopulates Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) drives on inference nodes with frequently used models and loads at several GB/s without the network, but it needs its own refresh policy as models update. Which versions those caches hold, and how a new version replaces an old one in production, belongs to the release process of @sec-ml-operations-model-deployment-b9b9.

### Multi-model serving {#sec-model-serving-multimodel-serving-a9c1}

Dedicating an entire GPU to each regional model, A/B candidate, or ensemble stage leaves most of the fleet idle whenever traffic to individual models is uneven, yet packing several models onto one GPU without coordination risks out-of-memory crashes and noisy-neighbor latency spikes. Production systems therefore share a single machine across multiple models\index{Multi-model serving!GPU memory management}, making GPU memory capacity and bandwidth isolation the primary constraints. How a server manages that shared memory depends on whether models fit in VRAM simultaneously. When the combined footprint exceeds device capacity, time-multiplexing\index{Time-multiplexing!model swapping} loads one model at a time and swaps weights on demand as routing changes, keeping implementation simple at the cost of swap latency. When several models fit together, memory sharing\index{Memory!sharing, GPU multi-model} partitions GPU memory among them so that more models remain resident without swapping, even though each model receives a smaller concurrency budget. Across both regimes, model virtualization\index{Model virtualization!lifecycle management}—as implemented by frameworks like Triton—decouples model lifecycle from application code by exposing repository and control APIs that load, unload, and version models dynamically [@nvidia_triton; @nvidiaTritonModelRepository; @nvidiaTritonModelManagement]. Which policy wins depends on the arrival mix. Steady traffic across models favors keeping them concurrently resident, whereas bursty, model-specific traffic favors time-multiplexing with explicit preloading to balance average latency against GPU utilization.

#### Partitioning one GPU across models {#sec-model-serving-multistream-execution-1b1f}

When multiple models or multiple instances of the same model must run concurrently on a single GPU, the hardware must partition resources between them. NVIDIA's Multi-Instance GPU[^fn-mig-gpu-partitioning]\index{MIG!hardware isolation} technology enables hardware-level isolation, dividing a data-center GPU such as the H100\index{H100!MIG partitioning} into up to seven independent GPU instances, each with dedicated memory and compute resources [@nvidiaMigUserGuide]. On GPUs without MIG, CUDA stream scheduling permits overlapping or time-multiplexed work without hardware partitioning. The choice depends on whether consistent latency with MIG or maximum utilization with shared streams is the priority.

[^fn-mig-gpu-partitioning]: **MIG (multi-instance GPU)**\index{MIG!multi-model serving}: Introduced with NVIDIA's A100 [@NVIDIA2020] and documented across supported data-center GPUs [@nvidiaMigUserGuide], MIG partitions a single physical GPU into independent instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources; unlike software sharing (MPS or time-slicing), MIG provides hardware-level isolation between partitions. The trade-off is granularity, because partitions must follow fixed profiles, so resources cannot be divided arbitrarily. For multi-model serving, MIG reduces noisy-neighbor risk on shared hardware, while per-model SLO guarantees still depend on scheduler policy, load, and the selected partition profile.

#### Model swapping and host memory {#sec-model-serving-model-swapping-host-memory-c54f}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: model-swap-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MODEL SWAP TIME
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Model swapping and host memory discussion
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the latency cost of model swapping.
# │ Show: That a reference model swap over PCIe takes hundreds of milliseconds.
# │ How: Load the reusable model-loading scenario and PCIe Gen4 bandwidth,
# │      then calculate transfer duration.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class ModelSwapCalc:
    """Quantifies the latency cost of swapping a reference model over PCIe Gen4."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    loading_scenario = ReferenceStats.ModelLoading
    model_size = loading_scenario.PcieSwapReferenceModelSize
    pcie_bw = Hardware.Cloud.A100.interconnect.bandwidth  # PCIe Gen4 x16 bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    model_swap = transfer_time(model_size, pcie_bw)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(round(model_swap.to(ms).magnitude, 1) == 312.5, f"Expected 312.5 ms model swap time, got {model_swap}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    model_size_gb_str = fmt_memory(model_size, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    pcie_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(pcie_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    model_swap_ms_str = fmt_time(model_swap, 'millisecond', precision=1, commas=False)
```

When the aggregate size of all models exceeds GPU memory capacity, the serving system must swap models between host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) and device memory (VRAM)\index{VRAM!device memory} on demand. This introduces a new latency component determined by the PCIe bus bandwidth\index{Bandwidth!PCIe, model swapping}. For a `{python} ModelSwapCalc.model_size_gb_str` model on PCIe Gen4 x16 (`{python} ModelSwapCalc.pcie_bw_gb_per_s_str` theoretical bandwidth), loading takes at least `{python} ModelSwapCalc.model_swap_ms_str` before deserialization, graph setup, or warmup. This raw transfer latency dwarfs a tight service-level objective such as a 50 ms deadline by more than $6\times$, rendering on-demand model swapping unviable on the interactive request path.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_model_serving_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal millisecond scale with a dashed red 50 ms SLO marker far left of a red model-load dot labeled 312.5 ms, with the region past the SLO shaded light red."}

*Model loading lands far outside a tight serving SLO.*
:::

To accelerate this transfer path, systems keep the weights in pinned memory\index{Pinned memory!DMA transfer} (page-locked host RAM). The GPU's DMA copy engines require the source pages to stay at fixed physical addresses for the whole transfer, but ordinary heap memory is pageable, and the operating system may relocate or swap its pages at any time. A transfer from a pageable buffer therefore takes two stages: the CPU first copies the data into a pinned staging buffer, and the DMA engine then moves that buffer across PCIe. Allocating model weights with `cudaHostAlloc` removes the CPU staging copy; achieved bandwidth still depends on transfer size, memory locality, and contention. What serving adds is a capacity trade-off. Pinned memory cannot be paged out or reclaimed by the OS under memory pressure, so every pinned model holds its share of physical host RAM until it is released. High-throughput serving systems therefore pin active model weights and I/O ring buffers while leaving standby model checkpoints in pageable memory.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Pinned memory and the DMA staging copy it avoids are established in @sec-ml-frameworks-os-interface.
:::

### Training-serving skew {#sec-model-serving-trainingserving-skew-7b99}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Training-serving skew and the consistency imperative it violates are established in @sec-data-engineering-ensuring-trainingserving-consistency-c683.
:::

Loading the exact checkpoint that training produced still does not guarantee that the server computes the same function if the host pipeline transforms raw inputs differently before those weights ever run. A model that performed well during validation degrades silently in production whenever training-serving skew\index{Training-serving skew!silent accuracy degradation} causes the two paths to compute different features from the same raw input while every latency and error-rate dashboard stays green. The consistency requirement belongs to the data pipeline; serving is where a violation surfaces, and because the divergence is measurable on identical inputs without labels (principle \ref{pri-training-serving-skew}), it is also one of the most preventable failures. @Sec-ml-operations-trainingserving-skew-diagnosis-prevention-9dc1 catalogs the skew categories and the method that detects each. The serving-specific manifestation of skew is **preprocessing divergence**\index{Preprocessing!divergence, training vs. serving}: the real-time inference pipeline processes raw data differently than the batch training pipeline, a common failure mode when training uses Python/Pandas while serving uses C++/Java or optimized inference servers.

::: {#exmp-model-serving-resnet-50-image-preprocessing-skew .callout-example title="ResNet-50: Image preprocessing skew"}

**Scenario**: ResNet-50 vision serving models experience silent prediction accuracy degradation between offline training and online serving pipelines.

**Diagnosis**: The serving pipeline implemented C++/OpenCV preprocessing (`cv2.INTER_LINEAR`, BGR order) while training used Python/PIL (`PIL.BILINEAR`, RGB order, different normalization constants).

**Systems lesson**: Preprocessing divergence causes silent training-serving skew without raising runtime exceptions. Standardizing data transformation pipelines across training and serving environments prevents input distribution corruption.

:::

A replica that loads quickly, runs predictably, and computes what training computed completes fixed-output serving. Every workload so far, however, has treated a request as one completed prediction. The fastest-growing category of serving workloads violates this assumption entirely. Large language models generate outputs token by token, with each token depending on every previous one. A single request may produce hundreds or thousands of tokens over seconds of elapsed time, yet must feel responsive from the first token onward. The shift from *fixed-output* to *variable-length, streaming-output* serving reopens each tool developed so far, from the latency budget to the runtime.

## LLM Serving {#sec-model-serving-llm-serving-b8bf}

An image classifier returns a single class vector in a few milliseconds and immediately frees its activation buffers, whereas a conversational LLM streams hundreds of tokens over several seconds while holding a growing key-value cache in GPU memory. LLMs\index{LLM serving!token generation} make three properties far more prominent than in fixed-output serving. *Autoregressive generation*[^fn-autoregressive-decoding-serving] means that each token depends on all previous tokens, which makes output inherently sequential. *Variable-length output* means that response length is unknown at request time, which complicates fixed-batch assumptions. *Stateful memory* means that the key-value cache grows with each generated token, which creates dynamic memory pressure. Each property strains a different tool from the preceding sections: sequential generation splits the latency budget into phases, unknown output length breaks fixed-batch scheduling, and the growing cache makes memory capacity, not arithmetic, the limit on concurrency. The p50, p95, and p99 metrics used for classification serving still matter, but they apply separately to the initial prompt processing and to the subsequent token generation. The same principles of queuing theory, batching trade-offs, and latency budgets remain applicable; LLM serving adds domain-specific techniques atop them.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Prefill, small-batch autoregressive decode, and the KV cache that every decode step reads are established in @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1.
:::

[^fn-autoregressive-decoding-serving]: **Autoregressive**\index{Autoregressive model!autoregressive, serial bottleneck}: From Greek *auto-* (self) and Latin *regressus* (a going back), since the output "regresses" on itself; George Udny Yule introduced autoregressive models in 1927 for analyzing sunspot cycles. In language modeling, each output token conditions on all previously generated tokens, creating a serial dependency that prevents the parallelism exploited during training. Decode is often weight-bandwidth-bound at small batches; larger batches amortize the weight stream and can shift the bottleneck toward compute or KV-cache traffic [@pope2023efficiently].

The chapter's second service carries the section. GPT-2 XL, the bandwidth-bound lighthouse, anchors the metrics, the decode floor, speculative decoding, and the energy per generated token, because its weight stream sets each of them. Llama 3 8B, introduced with the running cases, carries the cache budget, paging, and prefix reuse, because its longer contexts make memory capacity rather than bandwidth the constraint that binds first.

### Performance metrics: TTFT and TPOT {#sec-model-serving-performance-metrics-ttft-tpot-b009}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_model_serving_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A roofline silhouette: a blue memory-bound slope rising to a dashed ridge, then a flat orange compute-bound ceiling. A prefill dot sits on the orange ceiling; a low-batch decode dot sits on the blue slope."}

*Prefill and low-batch decode often face different resource limits.*
:::

A single end-to-end latency number cannot distinguish a chat response that begins streaming in 100 ms and flows at reading speed from one that leaves the user staring at a blank screen for two and a half seconds before dumping the entire paragraph at once. Because generative models emit a stream of tokens rather than a single output tensor, serving systems split latency into time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT). TPOT is the average of a request's inter-token latencies (ITL), as defined in @sec-benchmarking-token-latency-ttft-tpot-4e1a. In serving, each metric belongs to one phase. *Prefill* (processing the prompt and populating its KV cache) sets TTFT\index{Time to first token!prefill phase} and is often compute-bound, while *decode* (generating output) sets TPOT\index{Time per output token!decode phase} and is often bandwidth-bound at small batches. A low TTFT therefore does not mean a fast model. A model can have a fast TTFT but a sluggish TPOT (if the memory wall $(\Bandwidth)$ is the bottleneck), leading to a frustrating user experience where the answer starts quickly but "stutters" thereafter. Because these metrics capture distinct aspects of the user experience, interactive services set separate targets for TTFT, TPOT or ITL, and aggregate throughput.

::: {#psp-model-serving-llm-serving-latency-targets .callout-perspective title="LLM serving latency targets"}

Interactive LLM services usually need separate SLOs for responsiveness, generation fluidity, and fleet throughput. The following values are illustrative targets rather than universal requirements:

- **TTFT**: $<$ 500 ms (for a 1000-token prompt)
- **TPOT**: $<$ 50 ms (equivalent to ~20 tokens/s, faster than human reading speed)
- **Throughput**: $>$ 1000 tokens/s aggregate across active serving replicas

A single "latency" number therefore hides the prefill/decode split. TTFT is the blank-screen budget, TPOT is the reading-flow budget, and aggregate service throughput, measured as tokens/s summed across active serving replicas, determines whether those targets hold under shared load.

:::

### The decode floor {#sec-model-serving-decode-floor-7d3a}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: gpt2-decode-floor-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GPT-2 XL CHAT SERVICE: PREFILL, DECODE FLOOR, AND BATCHED DECODE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-model-serving-decode-floor-7d3a and @eq-token-generation-time.
# │
# │ Goal: Put numbers on TTFT and TPOT for the chapter's bandwidth-bound
# │       lighthouse on the book's reference H100.
# │ Show: Prefill time for a 512-token prompt; batch-one weight-read floor;
# │       eager host submission time; per-token KV bytes (no grouped-query
# │       sharing); bytes and time per decode step at batch 1 and 32.
# │ How: Registry GPT-2 XL shape and H100 compute/bandwidth; runtime
# │      overheads from the frameworks chapter's dispatch model.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Ops, BYTES_FP16, GB, MB, KB, TB, second, millisecond, microsecond, byte, flop
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_time, fmt_flops, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_rate, fmt_count
from mlsysim.core.units import TFLOPs

class Gpt2DecodeFloor:
    """GPT-2 XL prefill and decode on one H100, eager vs. graph-captured."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    kernel_launch = Ops.RuntimeOverheads.KernelLaunch
    python_dispatch = Ops.RuntimeOverheads.PythonDispatch
    kernels_per_block = 12  # scenario assumption: eager kernels per transformer block (frameworks chapter count)
    context_tokens = 1024  # GPT-2 context window (architecture constant)
    prompt_tokens = 512  # scenario assumption: chat prompt length
    prefill_efficiency = 0.4  # scenario assumption: fraction of FP16 peak sustained in prefill
    batch_large = 32  # scenario assumption: concurrent sequences in a full decode batch

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = gpt2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    bw = h100.memory.bandwidth
    peak_fp16 = h100.compute.precision_flops["fp16_dense"]
    prefill_flops = gpt2.inference_flops * prompt_tokens
    ttft = (prefill_flops / (peak_fp16 * prefill_efficiency)).to(millisecond)
    floor_b1 = (weights / bw).to(millisecond)
    n_kernels = kernels_per_block * gpt2.layers
    host_time = (n_kernels * (kernel_launch + python_dispatch)).to(millisecond)
    host_ratio = (host_time / floor_b1).to("").magnitude
    intensity_b1 = (2 * flop / BYTES_FP16).to(flop / byte)
    ridge = (peak_fp16 / bw).to(flop / byte)
    kv_per_token = (2 * gpt2.layers * gpt2.hidden_dim * BYTES_FP16).to(byte)
    kv_per_seq = (kv_per_token * context_tokens).to(MB)
    step_bytes_b1 = (weights + kv_per_seq).to(GB)
    step_bytes_bn = (weights + batch_large * kv_per_seq).to(GB)
    step_b1 = (step_bytes_b1 / bw).to(millisecond)
    step_bn = (step_bytes_bn / bw).to(millisecond)
    rate_b1 = (1 / step_b1).to(1 / second).magnitude
    rate_bn = (batch_large / step_bn).to(1 / second).magnitude
    tpot_stretch = (step_bn / step_b1).to("").magnitude
    kv_share_bn = ((batch_large * kv_per_seq) / step_bytes_bn).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.8 < floor_b1.magnitude < 1.0, f"GPT-2 XL weight read should be ~0.9 ms on an H100, got {floor_b1}.")
    check(n_kernels == 576, f"Expected 576 eager kernels per decode step, got {n_kernels}.")
    check(intensity_b1.magnitude < ridge.magnitude / 100, "Batch-one decode must sit two orders of magnitude below the ridge.")
    check(abs(kv_per_token.to(KB).magnitude - 307.2) < 0.1, f"GPT-2 XL KV should be 307.2 KB per token, got {kv_per_token}.")
    check(kv_share_bn > 0.5, f"At batch 32 with full context, caches should exceed half the step's bytes, got {kv_share_bn:.2f}.")
    check(rate_bn > 5 * rate_b1, "Batching must raise aggregate token throughput several-fold.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights_gb_str = fmt_memory(weights, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(prompt_tokens, commas=True)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_count(context_tokens, commas=True)
    prefill_tflop_str = fmt_flops(prefill_flops, unit=TFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    prefill_eff_str = fmt_percent(prefill_efficiency, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    ttft_ms_str = fmt_time(ttft, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    floor_b1_ms_str = fmt_time(floor_b1, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    n_kernels_str = fmt_count(n_kernels, commas=False)
    host_ms_str = fmt_time(host_time, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    host_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(host_ratio), precision=0, commas=False)
    intensity_b1_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(intensity_b1, precision=0, commas=False)
    ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(round(ridge.magnitude) * flop / byte, precision=0, commas=False)
    kv_per_token_kb_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_token, unit=KB, precision=1, commas=False)
    kv_per_seq_mb_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_seq, unit=MB, precision=None, commas=False)
    batch_large_str = fmt_count(batch_large, commas=False)
    step_bytes_b1_gb_str = fmt_memory(step_bytes_b1, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    step_bytes_bn_gb_str = fmt_memory(step_bytes_bn, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    step_b1_ms_str = fmt_time(step_b1, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    step_bn_ms_str = fmt_time(step_bn, unit="millisecond", precision=1, commas=False)
    rate_b1_str = fmt_rate(round(rate_b1, -1), "tokens/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    rate_bn_str = fmt_rate(round(rate_bn, -2), "tokens/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    tpot_stretch_mult_str = fmt_multiple(tpot_stretch, precision=1, commas=False)
    kv_share_bn_str = fmt_percent(round(kv_share_bn, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

The chapter's bandwidth-bound lighthouse puts numbers on both phases. A GPT-2 XL chat request with a `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.prompt_tokens_str`-token prompt performs about `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.prefill_tflop_str` of prefill arithmetic, which an H100 sustaining `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.prefill_eff_str` of its FP16 peak completes in about `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.ttft_ms_str`, the model's share of TTFT. Each decode step then reads all `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.weights_gb_str` of FP16 weights to produce one token per active sequence. At batch one that read takes `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.floor_b1_ms_str`, so the model-side TPOT can be no shorter, however many arithmetic units the accelerator adds. The floor assumes the step is launched as one captured graph. Issued operation by operation from an eager framework, the same step spends about `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.host_ms_str` on the host submitting `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.n_kernels_str` kernels, roughly `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.host_mult_str` the weight read, which is why every decode floor in this chapter assumes the CUDA Graph capture that @sec-ml-frameworks-hybrid-approaches-jit-compilation-8954 developed.

Batch-one decode with FP16 weights runs at the weight-only arithmetic intensity of about `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.intensity_b1_str` that @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1 derived. The H100's ridge point sits near `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.ridge_str`, so the step is memory-bandwidth bound by more than two orders of magnitude [@pope2023efficiently]. @Eq-token-generation-time gives its floor per token, where $\DataVolume$ is the bytes the step reads and $\AcceleratorMemoryBandwidth$ is the accelerator's memory bandwidth:
$$ \DecodeTokenTimeFloor\approx \frac{\DataVolume}{\AcceleratorMemoryBandwidth} $$ {#eq-token-generation-time}
While decode remains bandwidth bound, every step pays to move every weight, in energy as well as in time, and adding compute cores yields little latency improvement. Faster memory (Machine), fewer bytes per parameter or a smaller model (Algorithm), or better batching and cache management change the bound.

Batching changes which bytes dominate. Each sequence also reads its own KV cache on every step. GPT-2 XL's attention heads each keep their own keys and values, with no grouped-query sharing, so its cache holds `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.kv_per_token_kb_str` per token of context, or `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.kv_per_seq_mb_str` for a full `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.context_tokens_str`-token context. Batching shares the weight read across sequences but not the cache reads. At batch one with a full context, a step moves `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.step_bytes_b1_gb_str` and takes `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.step_b1_ms_str`. At batch `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.batch_large_str` it moves `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.step_bytes_bn_gb_str`, `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.kv_share_bn_str` of it cache, and takes `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.step_bn_ms_str`. Aggregate throughput rises from about `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.rate_b1_str` to `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.rate_bn_str`, while each sequence's TPOT stretches by `{python} Gpt2DecodeFloor.tpot_stretch_mult_str`. The same trade between per-sequence cadence and aggregate throughput governs every scheduling technique that follows.

### Decoding strategies {#sec-model-serving-decoding-strategies-afe8}

Switching a chat endpoint from greedy decoding to four-way beam search quadruples both the arithmetic per step and the KV-cache memory each active user holds. The sampling algorithm executed at each step therefore shapes serving cost directly. Greedy decoding\index{Greedy decoding!LLM generation} takes the highest-scoring token and needs one forward pass per token, though it can fall into repetitive output because it never revisits an early choice. Beam search\index{Beam search!decoding strategy} keeps several candidate sequences and multiplies both computational work and KV-cache footprint by the beam width. Stochastic sampling\index{Sampling!temperature, top-k, top-p} scales the logits by a temperature and truncates the vocabulary with top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$\index{Top-k!sampling} or top-$\NucleusProbabilityMass$ nucleus sampling\index{Nucleus sampling!top-p} before drawing a token [@holtzman2020curious]. For the serving system, beam width multiplies the state each request holds, while the sampling variants add only a small per-step reduction whose cost depends on its kernel implementation and on the sequence-length distribution that continuous batching must absorb.

Interactive LLM services commonly return tokens as they are produced rather than waiting for complete generation. This streaming response\index{Streaming response!LLM serving} transforms the user experience. A two-second total generation feels responsive when tokens stream continuously, but feels broken when users stare at a blank screen for two seconds. Streaming requires infrastructure support for incremental responses and client-side rendering. Once generation streams token by token, the serving unit changes from one fixed-output prediction to a stateful sequence whose length is unknown when it is admitted and whose memory footprint grows on every step. The unknown length breaks the fixed-batch scheduling developed for fixed-output models, and the growing state turns accelerator memory into the next constraint.

### Continuous batching {#sec-model-serving-continuous-batching-8bb6}

An autoregressive\index{Autoregressive model!token generation} request finishes only when it emits an end-of-sequence token, so its length is revealed one step at a time. Extending the request-level dynamic batching of @sec-model-serving-throughput-optimization-18d1 to an entire generation cycle keeps batch membership fixed until every sequence finishes. When sequence lengths vary, this static commitment degrades accelerator efficiency. If one sequence in a batch of eight finishes after ten tokens while others require 100 tokens, 90 percent of the compute and memory bandwidth allocated to that sequence slot is wasted on padding tokens or masked dummy operations while awaiting the slowest sequence\index{Sequence length variability!batch waste} [@yu2022orca].

**Continuous batching**\index{Continuous batching!LLM serving}[^fn-continuous-batching-llm] (also called iteration-level batching) eliminates this idle-slot waste by rescheduling batch composition at each decoding iteration [@yu2022orca; @kwon2023]. Rather than committing to a static batch that persists across hundreds of forward passes, the serving engine re-evaluates batch membership at every token-generation step. When a sequence emits its end-of-sequence token, the scheduler immediately reclaims that execution slot, admitting an arriving request into the batch for the subsequent forward pass. Active sequences continue decoding without interruption, maintaining high accelerator utilization across variable-length workloads.

[^fn-continuous-batching-llm]: **Continuous batching**\index{Continuous batching!scheduling granularity}: NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM calls the same technique "in-flight batching" [@nvidiaTensorRtLlm]. Request-level batching commits to a fixed batch for an entire generation sequence (potentially hundreds of iterations), while continuous batching reschedules at every token-generation step, a contrast that parallels preemptive OS process scheduling versus run-to-completion.

Serving runtimes such as vLLM[^fn-vllm-page-table] and TensorRT-LLM improve throughput via two mechanisms: reclaiming wasted compute from completed sequences and shortening queue wait times for new arrivals [@kwon2023; @nvidiaTensorRtLlm]. However, admitting new requests dynamically creates a systems collision between prompt prefill and token decoding. Long-prompt prefill often exposes high arithmetic intensity and can occupy the GPU for tens of milliseconds. Low-batch decoding often has less weight reuse and is memory-bandwidth bound, advancing one token per active sequence at a time. When an engine executes a prefill in the same iteration as active decodes, the ongoing decode streams stall, causing severe spikes in inter-token latency. Sarathi-Serve resolves this interference through chunked prefill and stall-free batching [@agrawal2024sarathi]. By splitting long prompts into fixed-size chunks (e.g., 512 tokens) and co-scheduling a single chunk alongside active decode requests per step, the scheduler limits the prefill work admitted per iteration, reducing interference with active decodes. Measured iteration times determine the resulting token cadence.

[^fn-vllm-page-table]: **vLLM (virtual large language model (LLM))**\index{vLLM!virtual memory analogy}: An open-source serving system that enables continuous batching via its PagedAttention algorithm [@kwon2023]. Keeping KV-cache waste low lets it serve larger effective batches on the same hardware.

#### Speculative decoding {#sec-model-serving-speculative-decoding-b52e}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: speculative-decoding-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SPECULATIVE DECODING ON THE GPT-2 XL SERVICE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-model-serving-speculative-decoding-b52e and @eq-speculative-tokens.
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify how many tokens one target weight stream yields when a small
# │       draft model proposes several tokens.
# │ Show: Expected tokens per verification pass, time per generated token,
# │       and the speedup over plain batch-one decode.
# │ How: Bandwidth-bound step times for GPT-2 XL (target) and GPT-2 Small
# │      (draft) on an H100; acceptance rate is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, BYTES_FP16, MB, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_time, fmt_multiple, fmt_count, fmt_percent

class SpeculativeDecoding:
    """Draft-and-verify decoding for GPT-2 XL with a GPT-2 Small draft on one H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    target = Models.Language.GPT2
    draft = Models.Language.GPT2_Small
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    draft_tokens = 4  # scenario assumption: tokens proposed per round
    acceptance = 0.7  # scenario assumption: per-token acceptance probability

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    bw = h100.memory.bandwidth
    target_step = (target.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16) / bw).to(millisecond)
    draft_weights = draft.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    draft_step = (draft_weights / bw).to(millisecond)
    draft_cost = draft_tokens * draft_step
    expected_tokens = (1 - acceptance ** (draft_tokens + 1)) / (1 - acceptance)
    round_time = target_step + draft_cost
    per_token = round_time / expected_tokens
    speedup = (target_step / per_token).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(1 < expected_tokens < draft_tokens + 1, f"Expected tokens must lie between 1 and k+1, got {expected_tokens:.2f}.")
    check(draft_cost < target_step, "The draft's reads must cost less than one target pass.")
    check(1.5 < speedup < 3.0, f"Speedup should be about 2x, got {speedup:.2f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    draft_tokens_str = fmt_count(draft_tokens, commas=False)
    acceptance_str = fmt_percent(acceptance, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    draft_weights_mb_str = fmt_memory(draft_weights, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    target_step_ms_str = fmt_time(target_step, unit="millisecond", precision=2, commas=False)
    draft_cost_ms_str = fmt_time(draft_cost, unit="millisecond", precision=2, commas=False)
    expected_tokens_str = fmt_count(expected_tokens, precision=1, commas=False, allow_fractional=True)
    per_token_ms_str = fmt_time(per_token, unit="millisecond", precision=2, commas=False)
    speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup, precision=1, commas=False)
```

Continuous batching and chunked prefill keep decode batches full and their cadence steady, but at small batch each generated token still pays for one full weight stream. Speculative decoding[^fn-speculative-decoding-verification]\index{Speculative decoding!latency reduction}\index{Speculative decoding!draft model verification} attacks that bound directly. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies the whole proposal in one parallel pass, so a single weight stream can yield more than one accepted token. Evaluated T5-XXL workloads achieved roughly 2--3$\times$ speedups [@leviathan2023speculative], though the gain depends on how often the target model accepts the draft.

[^fn-speculative-decoding-verification]: **Speculative decoding**\index{Speculative decoding!throughput}: Parallel verification is possible because the draft has already committed to all $\DraftTokenCount$ candidate tokens, so the target can score the whole block in one causal-attention forward pass, as it scores a prompt during prefill, rather than in $\DraftTokenCount$ sequential steps [@leviathan2023speculative]. The technique removes serial steps at the runtime layer without changing the model architecture.

If the draft proposes $\DraftTokenCount$ tokens and the target accepts each with probability $\DraftAcceptanceRate$, independently of the others [@leviathan2023speculative], one verification pass yields on average the number of tokens in @eq-speculative-tokens, which counts the accepted draft tokens plus the one token the target always contributes:
$$\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens per target pass}] = \frac{1-\DraftAcceptanceRate^{\DraftTokenCount+1}}{1-\DraftAcceptanceRate}$$ {#eq-speculative-tokens}

Verifying $\DraftTokenCount+1$ positions costs the target about one weight stream, because at batch one the pass remains bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. For the GPT-2 XL service, a GPT-2 Small draft with `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.draft_weights_mb_str` of FP16 weights proposes `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.draft_tokens_str` tokens per round, spending `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.draft_cost_ms_str` on draft reads against `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.target_step_ms_str` for the target's verification pass. At an assumed acceptance rate of `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.acceptance_str`, a round yields `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.expected_tokens_str` tokens on average, so the time per generated token falls from `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.target_step_ms_str` to `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.per_token_ms_str`, a `{python} SpeculativeDecoding.speedup_mult_str` speedup. The gain shrinks as acceptance falls or as the batch grows. A full batch already shares each weight stream across many sequences, and verifying several positions per sequence then consumes arithmetic that a batch-one step left idle but a full batch does not.

#### PagedAttention {#sec-model-serving-pagedattention-b8d4}

Keeping decode batches full, however, shifts the primary serving bottleneck to memory management. Because transformer generation appends attention states at every step, the KV cache for each active request grows dynamically in accelerator HBM. When sequences of varying lengths share memory, contiguous allocation produces severe external fragmentation. If a completed 100-token sequence releases its cache, an arriving 150-token request cannot occupy that freed memory because it requires a larger contiguous address range. Over time, physical memory fractures into small, noncontiguous gaps, preventing new sequences from launching even when total unallocated capacity appears sufficient. Together with the over-reservation of contiguous allocators, this memory fragmentation\index{Memory fragmentation!KV cache} can waste 60 to 80 percent of KV-cache memory in naive implementations [@kwon2023], severely limiting the concurrent batch size that determines serving throughput.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_model_serving_margin_002.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars: the contiguous-allocation bar carries a wide red wasted segment; the paged-allocation bar below shows only a thin red sliver, the rest used."}

*PagedAttention recovers the KV-cache waste of contiguous allocation.*
:::

**PagedAttention**\index{PagedAttention!memory fragmentation solution},[^fn-paged-attention-memory] introduced in vLLM, resolves this fragmentation by applying operating system virtual memory paging to accelerator memory [@kwon2023]. In static contiguous allocation, reserving maximum sequence length memory up front causes internal waste, while freed regions may be too small or poorly placed to satisfy a new contiguous reservation. Instead of allocating one contiguous region per sequence, PagedAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks mapped through a block table. A sequence's cache can therefore occupy noncontiguous physical blocks. When a sequence completes, its blocks return to a free pool for reuse. Rather than copying noncontiguous blocks into a temporary contiguous buffer before computing attention, a specialized PagedAttention CUDA kernel traverses the block table directly, staging noncontiguous blocks into on-chip SRAM during query-key multiplication. By eliminating external fragmentation and bounding internal waste to each sequence's last, partially filled block, PagedAttention reduced KV-cache waste below 4 percent in the reported evaluation and enabled substantially higher batch concurrency on the same accelerator hardware [@kwon2023]. Paging decides where cache blocks live, however. It does not reduce how many blocks each sequence needs, and that number grows with every generated token.

[^fn-paged-attention-memory]: **PagedAttention**\index{PagedAttention!memory efficiency}: The name directly references OS virtual memory paging, first implemented on the Atlas computer at Manchester (1962) to solve the same class of allocation problem, in which programs needed more memory than physically available, and contiguous allocation wasted space [@kilburn1962onelevel]. Introduced at SOSP 2023, PagedAttention applies this six-decade-old abstraction to GPU KV-cache memory; in its evaluation, the recovered memory enabled 2--4$\times$ higher throughput on the same hardware [@kwon2023].

### Memory and KV cache {#sec-model-serving-memory-kv-cache-d1ea}

Even after PagedAttention eliminates fragmentation waste, thirty-two long-context conversations can exhaust an 80 GB GPU's memory when the quantized model weights themselves occupy less than half the device. The KV cache\index{KV cache!LLM memory}\index{KV cache!sequence length scaling}, the per-sequence store of attention keys and values defined in @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1, grows linearly with sequence length. Prefill creates cache entries for every prompt token, and each decoded token appends another entry, so a request's footprint is set by its prompt length plus the tokens it has generated so far. Summed across concurrent variable-length sequences, this dynamic state can exceed the model weights and dominate available accelerator memory, which is why the remaining memory levers either reuse cache state across requests or move it off the accelerator.

#### KV budget {#sec-model-serving-kv-budget-e81c}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-budget-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KV-CACHE BUDGET ON ONE H100
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-model-serving-kv-budget-e81c and @fig-kv-cache-growth.
# │
# │ Goal: Show that cache, not weights, bounds concurrency once contexts grow.
# │ Show: Llama 3 8B FP16 KV bytes per token and per 8K-token conversation;
# │       resident conversations after FP16 weights on an 80 GiB H100; the
# │       70-billion-parameter scale-up (INT4 weights, batch 32 crossing).
# │ How: Registry layer, KV-head, and hidden dimensions; registry H100 capacity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, BYTES_FP16, BYTES_INT4, GB, GiB, KB, byte
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_count, fmt_multiple

class KvBudget:
    """KV-cache budget for Llama 3 8B and a 70B-class model on one H100."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    llama8 = Models.Language.Llama3_8B
    llama70 = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    context_tokens = 8192  # scenario assumption: one long conversation (8K tokens)
    batch_large = 32  # scenario assumption: concurrent conversations for the 70B scale-up

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    capacity = h100.memory.capacity
    head_dim = llama8.hidden_dim // llama8.heads
    kv_per_token = (2 * llama8.layers * llama8.kv_heads * head_dim * BYTES_FP16).to(byte)
    kv_per_seq = (kv_per_token * context_tokens).to(GB)
    weights8 = llama8.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16).to(GB)
    free8 = (capacity - weights8).to(GB)
    n_seq = int((free8 / kv_per_seq).to("").magnitude)
    mha_ratio = llama8.heads // llama8.kv_heads
    kv70_per_token = (2 * llama70.layers * llama70.kv_heads * (llama70.hidden_dim // llama70.heads) * BYTES_FP16).to(byte)
    weights70 = llama70.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT4).to(GB)
    free70 = (capacity - weights70).to(GB)
    crossing70 = (free70 / (batch_large * kv70_per_token)).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(kv_per_token.magnitude == 131072, f"Llama 3 8B KV should be 131,072 B per token, got {kv_per_token}.")
    check(1.0 < kv_per_seq.magnitude < 1.1, f"An 8K conversation should hold ~1.07 GB, got {kv_per_seq}.")
    check(50 < n_seq < 80, f"Resident 8K conversations should be in the 60s, got {n_seq}.")
    check(4000 < crossing70 < 5500, f"Batch-32 70B crossing should be near 4.8K tokens, got {crossing70:.0f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    heads_str = fmt_count(llama8.heads, commas=False)
    mha_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(mha_ratio, precision=0, commas=False)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_count(context_tokens, commas=True)
    kv_per_seq_gb_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_seq, unit=GB, precision=2, commas=False)
    weights8_gb_str = fmt_memory(weights8, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    capacity_gib_str = fmt_memory_capacity(capacity, unit=GiB, commas=False)
    capacity_gb_str = fmt_memory(capacity, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    free8_gb_str = fmt_memory(free8, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    n_seq_str = fmt_count(n_seq, commas=False)
    weights70_gb_str = fmt_memory(weights70, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    free70_gb_str = fmt_memory(free70, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    batch_large_str = fmt_count(batch_large, commas=False)
    crossing70_str = fmt_count(round(crossing70, -2), commas=True)
```

Once contexts grow, the cache rather than the weights sets how many conversations one accelerator can hold, and Llama 3 8B makes the budget concrete. Each token stores a key vector and a value vector in every layer for every key-value head. Storing 16-bit Key and Value tensors across $\LayerCount=32$ layers with $\KvHeadCount=8$ grouped-query attention heads of dimension $\AttentionHeadDimension=128$ requires $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 131{,}072\text{ bytes} \approx 131\text{ KB}$ per token per sequence. Grouped-query attention [@dubey2024llama] lets the model's `{python} KvBudget.heads_str` query heads share those key-value heads, which cuts the cache by `{python} KvBudget.mha_ratio_mult_str` relative to full multi-head attention. An `{python} KvBudget.context_tokens_str`-token conversation therefore holds `{python} KvBudget.kv_per_seq_gb_str`. With `{python} KvBudget.weights8_gb_str` of FP16 weights resident on an H100 whose `{python} KvBudget.capacity_gib_str` datasheet capacity is `{python} KvBudget.capacity_gb_str` in the decimal units used for tensor footprints, about `{python} KvBudget.free8_gb_str` remains for caches before runtime workspace, room for about `{python} KvBudget.n_seq_str` such conversations at once. The weights are a fixed cost; every additional conversation, and every additional thousand tokens of context, draws on the same remainder.

Larger models make the cache the binding constraint sooner. For a 70-billion-parameter-class model with grouped-query attention, 4-bit weights consume `{python} KvBudget.weights70_gb_str` of the same H100, leaving `{python} KvBudget.free70_gb_str` for FP16 cache before runtime workspace. A batch of `{python} KvBudget.batch_large_str` conversations exhausts that budget at roughly `{python} KvBudget.crossing70_str` tokens of context, so serving engines trade concurrent batch size against context length to avoid out-of-memory failures (@fig-kv-cache-growth).

::: {#fig-kv-cache-growth fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The KV-Cache Explosion**: FP16 KV-cache usage vs. context length for a 70-billion-parameter-class model with GQA. On the modeled H100's 80 GB of HBM (85.9 GB decimal), 35.3 GB of INT4 weights leave 50.6 GB for KV cache before runtime overhead. Batch size 32 reaches that cache budget at roughly 4.8k tokens, forcing a trade-off between batch size and context length." fig-alt="Line chart of FP16 KV-cache size against context length for batch sizes 1, 4, 16, and 32. All four lines rise linearly, with steeper slopes for larger batches. A red dashed horizontal line marks the cache budget remaining after the INT4 weights on the modeled H100; batch size 32 crosses it near 4.8k tokens. The region above the budget line is shaded red and labeled Out of Memory (OOM) Zone."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KV-CACHE GROWTH FIGURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-kv-cache-growth—introduces the KV-cache memory bottleneck
# │          for LLM serving with long contexts and large batch sizes
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate that KV-cache memory grows linearly with context length
# │       and batch size, exhausting the cache budget after resident weights.
# │ Show: KV-cache size (GB) vs. context length (tokens) for batch sizes 1, 4,
# │       16, 32; post-weight cache budget annotated; OOM zone shaded.
# │ How: Compute KV cache bytes = 2 × layers × d_model × seq × batch × bytes
# │      ÷ gqa_ratio; convert to GB; plot per-batch-size using book.tools.figures.style palette.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Demonstrate that KV-cache memory grows linearly with context length
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 3.9))
# =============================================================================
# PLOT: The KV-Cache Explosion
# =============================================================================

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
seq_len = np.linspace(0, 32000, 100)
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models

_m70b = Models.Language.Llama3_70B  # 70-billion-parameter class, FP16
layers, d_model, bytes_per_param = _m70b.layers, _m70b.hidden_dim, BYTES_FP16.to(byte).magnitude
gqa_ratio = _m70b.heads // _m70b.kv_heads  # Grouped Query Attention (query heads / KV heads)

def get_kv_gb(batch, seq):
    # KV cache size = 2 * layers * d_model * seq * batch * bytes_per_param/gqa_ratio
    bytes_total = (2 * layers * d_model * seq * batch * bytes_per_param) / gqa_ratio
    return (bytes_total * byte).to(GB).magnitude

batches = [1, 4, 16, 32]
colors = [COLORS['BlueLine'], COLORS['GreenLine'], COLORS['OrangeLine'], COLORS['VioletLine']]

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for b, c in zip(batches, colors):
    gb = get_kv_gb(b, seq_len)
    ax.plot(seq_len, gb, label=f'Batch Size {b}', color=c, linewidth=2)

device_capacity = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.capacity
int4_weights = _m70b.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT4)
limit_gb = (device_capacity - int4_weights).to(GB).magnitude
ax.axhline(limit_gb, color=COLORS['RedLine'], linestyle='--', linewidth=2)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.text(
    27000,
    limit_gb + 2,
    f"KV Budget after INT4 Weights ({limit_gb:.0f} GB)",
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    fontweight='bold',
    ha='center',
    fontsize=9,
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)
ax.axhspan(limit_gb, 140, color=COLORS['RedL'], alpha=0.2)
ax.text(
    27000,
    100,
    "Out of Memory\n(OOM) Zone",
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    ha='center',
    fontsize=10,
    fontweight='bold',
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)

ax.annotate(
    "Linear Growth",
    xy=(15000, get_kv_gb(4, 15000)),
    xytext=(11000, 34),
    arrowprops=dict(facecolor=COLORS['primary'], arrowstyle='->'),
    fontsize=9,
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)

ax.set_xlabel('Context Length (Tokens)')
ax.set_ylabel('KV Cache Size (GB) [FP16]')
ax.set_xlim(0, 32000)
ax.set_ylim(0, 120)
ax.set_xticks([0, 8000, 16000, 24000, 32000])
ax.set_xticklabels(['0', '8k', '16k', '24k', '32k'])
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9, frameon=True, facecolor='white', framealpha=0.95, edgecolor='gray', fancybox=True, borderpad=0.6)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

A model whose weights and cache do not fit one accelerator, even at reduced precision, can still be served from one machine by splitting it across the node's accelerators with the model parallelism of @sec-model-training-model-parallelism-c97e. Serving usually favors tensor parallelism\index{Tensor parallelism!serving}. Pipeline stages also fit, but every decoded token must pass through each stage in turn, which adds latency to every step. Tensor parallelism instead puts every accelerator to work on every layer, and each accelerator holds a slice of the weights and of the KV cache. A 70-billion-parameter-class model at 16-bit precision, whose weights alone exceed one H100's memory, therefore fits across the accelerators of one node with room left for cache. The cost is a collective operation after each layer's matrix multiplications. On NVLink that exchange is small next to the layer's compute; over PCIe or a network it would dominate each decode step. A serving engine therefore keeps one model's tensor-parallel group inside a single node and meets higher volume by replicating whole groups across machines rather than stretching one group across them.

#### Prefix caching and memory offloading {#sec-model-serving-prefix-caching-offloading}

Many requests carry identical prefixes, and recomputing their cache entries wastes both prefill compute and memory. **Prefix caching**\index{Prefix caching!KV cache reuse} stores the KV states of common instruction prefixes (such as a 2,000-token system prompt or a shared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context), allowing independent requests to reuse the prefill result for an identical prefix. For $\SharedPrefixRequestCount$ requests sharing a prefix of $\SharedPrefixLength$ tokens, the avoided prefill work is roughly $(\SharedPrefixRequestCount-1)\SharedPrefixLength$ token steps, subject to cache hits, eviction, and implementation overhead. For multi-turn conversations, the same principle lets a subsequent turn process only the new suffix after reusing compatible prior state.

When the aggregate KV cache exceeds GPU VRAM, systems can use **KV cache offloading**\index{KV cache!offloading}. This strategy spills inactive or low-priority context windows to host CPU RAM or NVMe SSD, freeing VRAM for active generation. The reload cost is bounded below by bytes moved divided by PCIe or NVMe bandwidth, before software overhead and queueing are added. Offloading therefore prevents OOM failures and enables larger context windows, but it also creates affinity, invalidation, and hot-decode latency risks that must be budgeted explicitly.

### Session affinity constraints {#sec-model-serving-session-affinity-constraints-8b1f}

Prefix reuse and offloading both assume that the next turn of a conversation reaches the replica that holds its cache. Session affinity, routing successive requests from a client to the same physical replica, arises whenever serving state resides in local accelerator memory rather than being reconstructed on every invocation. In conversational models, this resident state is dominated by the KV cache\index{KV cache!session reuse}\index{KV cache!multi-turn conversations}. When turn $\ConversationTurnIndex$ executes on a replica, that replica's HBM retains the projected keys and values across all prior prompt and generation tokens. Routing turn $\ConversationTurnIndex+1$ to a different replica discards that local memory footprint, forcing the new node to recompute the entire prefix sequence from scratch. This redundant prefill consumes memory bandwidth and tensor-core cycles that would otherwise advance active decode iterations, directly inflating time-to-first-token.

A parallel physical constraint governs personalized serving using fine-tuned Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules\index{Personalized model!user adapters}: small per-user adapters, each a pair of low-rank matrices whose product is added to a frozen base weight matrix. While base-model weights remain pinned in device HBM, individual user adapters must be dynamically staged into memory. If incoming requests for a user scatter across multiple replicas, each node must repeatedly transfer adapter tensors over the host-to-device PCIe bus or fetch them across the network, displacing other active working sets in memory. Stateful preprocessing pipelines, such as tokenizer vocabularies and per-session normalization state, impose the same penalty, requiring redundant CPU-side allocations and cache rebuilds whenever execution moves across node boundaries.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Products of two low-rank matrices, and the storage and memory traffic they save relative to a full matrix, are established in @sec-model-compression-lowrank-factorization-955e.
:::

Strict affinity\index{Session affinity!sticky sessions} creates a direct conflict with dynamic batching. Continuous batch schedulers maximize accelerator throughput by packing concurrent requests into unified matrix multiplications, raising operational arithmetic intensity in proportion to batch size ($\ArithmeticIntensity\propto \BatchSize$). When requests are pinned to designated replicas, the scheduler's pool of batchable candidates fragments across the cluster. A replica assigned to an idle or low-concurrency user session must either process underfilled batches, collapsing arithmetic intensity back into the memory-bandwidth-bound regime, or stall waiting for affinity-matched tokens. To prevent this collapse in utilization, production routers use soft affinity\index{Soft affinity!load balancing}. Under soft affinity, the ingress gateway prioritizes the cache-holding replica when capacity allows, but sheds requests to alternate nodes when local queue delays exceed the physical latency required to transfer adapter weights or recompute prefix tokens.

::: {#psp-model-serving-llm-serving-beyond-fundamentals .callout-perspective title="LLM serving: Beyond the fundamentals"}

Each LLM serving technique answers one of two physical limits. The first is the decode bound, in which every generated token pays for a full weight stream at small batch. Continuous batching keeps decode batches full so each stream serves many sequences, chunked prefill keeps prompt processing from stalling that stream, and speculative decoding extracts more than one accepted token per stream. The second is the KV cache, which grows with sequence length and batch size and often exceeds the weights themselves; PagedAttention, prefix caching, offloading, and session affinity decide where it lives and how much of it can be reused. Weight-only quantization (such as INT4 weights with FP16 activations), the precision lever of @sec-model-serving-precision-selection-serving-55ba applied to the weight stream, addresses both at once, because it shrinks the bytes streamed per token and frees capacity for cache [@lin2023awq].

These LLM-specific optimizations build directly on core serving mechanics: queueing models govern scheduling timeouts, batching dynamics determine throughput-latency curves, and reduced precision bounds memory traffic. Advanced treatments extend these mechanics to multi-tenant prefix sharing across fleets and multi-node tensor-parallel execution.

:::

Every technique above changes how many sequences share each weight stream and how long each one holds its cache. Because an accelerator draws power whether a decode pass serves one sequence or a full batch, that same sharing directly governs the energy each generated token costs. Dividing node power by aggregate token throughput converts batching and prefix-caching gains into joules per token.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: carbon-cost-h100-tdp
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ H100 TDP FOR CARBON COST OF CHAT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "The Carbon Cost of a Chat" (~10 lines below)
# │
# │ Goal: Provide H100 TDP for the energy-per-token callout.
# │ Show: The power envelope of the H100 GPU.
# │ How: Retrieve TDP from Hardware Digital Twins.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.core.units import watt
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_power

class CarbonCostH100Tdp:
    """H100 TDP anchor for the carbon-cost-of-chat callout."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    h_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    h100_tdp_w_str = fmt_power(h_h100.tdp, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: carbon-cost-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CARBON COST OF CHAT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "The Carbon Cost of a Chat" - energy footprint of LLM serving
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the energy cost per LLM token.
# │ Show: That poor utilization causes about 6× higher energy consumption per token.
# │ How: Calculate J per token based on TDP and concurrent request volume.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, fmt_count, check, fmt_percent, fmt_rate, fmt_power, fmt_energy, fmt_multiple

class CarbonCostCalc:
    """Energy cost per LLM token: poor utilization causes about 6× higher J/token."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Energy anchors sourced from the mlsysim registry (ReferenceStats.EnergyAnchors).
    ENERGY_SMARTPHONE_CHARGE_J = ReferenceStats.EnergyAnchors.SmartphoneCharge
    ENERGY_BOILING_WATER_J = ReferenceStats.EnergyAnchors.BoilingWater
    cc_concurrent_requests_value = 114  # concurrent requests per H100
    cc_tokens_per_sec_req_value = 8 * (count / second)  # scenario assumption: decode tokens/s per request
    cc_host_overhead = 300 * watt  # scenario assumption: host server power overhead
    cc_response_tokens_value = 500  # typical response length
    cc_low_util_pct_value = 10  # poor utilization scenario (%)
    cc_idle_power = 300 * watt  # scenario assumption: GPU idle power

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    _h100_tdp = Hardware.Cloud.H100.tdp
    cc_total_tokens_sec = cc_concurrent_requests_value * cc_tokens_per_sec_req_value
    cc_total_power = _h100_tdp + cc_host_overhead
    cc_joules_per_token = cc_total_power / cc_total_tokens_sec
    cc_response_joules = cc_joules_per_token * cc_response_tokens_value * count
    cc_low_util_tokens_sec = cc_total_tokens_sec * (cc_low_util_pct_value / 100)
    cc_low_util_power = cc_idle_power + cc_host_overhead
    cc_low_util_joules = cc_low_util_power / cc_low_util_tokens_sec
    cc_low_util_ratio = (cc_low_util_joules / cc_joules_per_token).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        cc_total_tokens_sec.to(count / second).magnitude == 912,
        f"114 concurrent requests × 8 tokens/s should be 912 tokens/s, got {cc_total_tokens_sec.to(count / second).magnitude:.0f}",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    cc_concurrent_str = fmt(cc_concurrent_requests_value, precision=0, commas=False)
    cc_tokens_req_tokens_per_s_str = fmt_rate(cc_tokens_per_sec_req_value, 'tokens/s', precision=0, commas=False)
    cc_total_tokens_per_s_str = fmt_rate(round(cc_total_tokens_sec.to(count / second).magnitude), 'tokens/s', precision=0, commas=False)
    cc_host_overhead_w_str = fmt_power(cc_host_overhead, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
    cc_total_power_w_str = fmt_power(cc_total_power, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
    cc_joules_token_j_str = fmt_energy(cc_joules_per_token, unit=joule, precision=4, commas=False, per='token')
    cc_response_tokens_str = fmt_count(cc_response_tokens_value, label="token", commas=False)
    cc_response_joules_j_str = fmt_energy(cc_response_joules, unit=joule, precision=1, commas=False)
    cc_smartphone_j_str = fmt_energy(ENERGY_SMARTPHONE_CHARGE_J, unit=joule, precision=0)
    cc_boiling_j_str = fmt_energy(ENERGY_BOILING_WATER_J, unit=joule, precision=0)
    cc_low_util_pct_str = fmt_percent(cc_low_util_pct_value / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    cc_idle_power_w_str = fmt_power(cc_idle_power, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
    cc_low_util_joules_j_str = fmt_energy(cc_low_util_joules, unit=joule, precision=1, commas=False, per='token')
    cc_low_util_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(cc_low_util_ratio), precision=0, commas=False)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: chat-measured-anchor
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEASURED PRODUCTION PROMPT ENERGY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Systems insight of @nbk-carbon-chat below.
# │
# │ Goal: Set the scenario's per-response estimate beside a measured median.
# │ Show: 0.24 Wh ≈ 864 J for the median Gemini text prompt (full stack).
# │ How: Literature.Series.GeminiPromptEnergy (Table 1 full-stack total), in joules.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.core.units import Wh, joule
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_energy

class ChatMeasuredAnchor:
    """Measured full-stack energy of the median Gemini text prompt (Elsworth et al. 2025)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    _rows = Literature.Series.GeminiPromptEnergy.entries
    measured = sum(r["comprehensive_wh"] for r in _rows if r["comprehensive_counted"] == 1) * Wh

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    _ratio = (measured / CarbonCostCalc.cc_response_joules).to("").magnitude
    check(0.1 < _ratio < 10, "Prose says the measured median is the same order of magnitude as the scenario.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    measured_j_str = fmt_energy(measured.to(joule), unit=joule, precision=0, commas=False)
    measured_wh_str = fmt_energy(measured, unit=Wh, precision=2, commas=False)
```

::: {#nbk-carbon-chat .callout-notebook title="The energy cost of a chat"}

**Problem**: How much energy does an H100-backed chat service spend per generated token and for a response with `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_response_tokens_str`?

As LLMs scale, joules per token becomes a first-class operational metric alongside latency. Assuming the H100 draws its `{python} CarbonCostH100Tdp.h100_tdp_w_str` thermal design power (TDP), this scenario estimate follows from throughput and power [@choquette2023]:

1.  **Throughput**: `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_concurrent_str` concurrent requests $\times$ `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_tokens_req_tokens_per_s_str` per request ≈ `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_total_tokens_per_s_str`.
2.  **Power**: `{python} CarbonCostH100Tdp.h100_tdp_w_str` (GPU) + `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_host_overhead_w_str` (Host/Overhead) = `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_total_power_w_str`.
3.  **Energy per token**:
    `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_total_power_w_str` / `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_total_tokens_per_s_str` ≈ `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_joules_token_j_str`

```{=latex}
\vspace*{-1.2ex}
```
**Systems insight**: Under these assumptions, a response of `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_response_tokens_str` consumes ≈ `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_response_joules_j_str`. A measured production figure is of the same order. Google reports ≈ `{python} ChatMeasuredAnchor.measured_j_str` (`{python} ChatMeasuredAnchor.measured_wh_str`) for the median Gemini text prompt, counting host, idle-reserve, and facility energy, although the study does not state how long that prompt was [@elsworth2025measuring].

- For comparison, charging a smartphone consumes ≈ `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_smartphone_j_str`.
- Boiling a cup of water consumes ≈ `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_boiling_j_str`.

```{=latex}
\vspace*{-0.7ex}
```
The primary way to reduce J/token is to increase hardware utilization and eliminate redundant compute. If the GPU sits at `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_low_util_pct_str` utilization due to poor batching, it still draws ~`{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_idle_power_w_str` and the host adds `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_host_overhead_w_str`, causing energy per token to rise to `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_low_util_joules_j_str` (approximately `{python} CarbonCostCalc.cc_low_util_ratio_mult_str` the baseline). Architectural optimizations like prefix caching also skip the energy-intensive prefill phase for shared context, directly reducing the energy footprint of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and chat applications. The serving lesson is that efficiency is not only a latency or cost metric; it also determines how much energy each useful token consumes.

:::

::: {#psp-model-serving-looking-ahead-rise-inference-time-compute-system-2 .callout-perspective title="Looking ahead: Spending more compute per query"}

Every lever so far takes the number of tokens a request generates as given, and fixed-output serving minimizes latency ($\EndToEndRequestLatency \to 0$) for a fixed amount of work per request. Reasoning models and other inference-time-compute systems\index{Reasoning model!inference-time compute}\index{Inference-time compute!reasoning models} make that token count a choice: they deliberately spend more computation per query to improve answer quality, generating intermediate reasoning or search tokens before the visible answer. The optimization target then expands to include answer quality, and every extra reasoning token pays the decode costs this section derived. It adds one more step of decode work at the batch's cadence, holds one more KV-cache entry until the response ends, and takes its share of the joules per token. Answer quality now trades directly against TPOT, cache capacity, and energy per query.

:::

::: {#chk-model-serving-llm-serving-fundamentals .callout-checkpoint title="LLM serving fundamentals"}

LLM serving introduces constraints absent from traditional model serving.

- [ ] **TTFT vs. TPOT**: Contrast the distinct user experiences captured by TTFT and TPOT, explain why long-prompt prefill often exposes more arithmetic intensity than low-batch decode, and convert a 50 ms TPOT target into its tokens-per-second equivalent.
- [ ] **Continuous batching and PagedAttention**: Contrast static batching waste under variable sequence lengths against iteration-level scheduling, and explain how PagedAttention eliminates external fragmentation in the KV cache and bounds internal waste to a single partially filled block per sequence.
- [ ] **Memory wall**: Explain why adding compute units yields negligible latency improvement when token generation is bandwidth-bound, and identify how higher-bandwidth memory, model quantization, or batching alters the operating regime.
- [ ] **Prefix caching and offloading**: Explain how caching key-value activations for shared prompt prefixes eliminates redundant prefill compute, and evaluate the latency trade-offs that govern offloading KV caches to host system memory.
- [ ] **Joules per token**: Explain why energy consumption scales with generated sequence length, and how low hardware utilization inflates the energy cost per useful token.

:::

Every LLM serving optimization ultimately decides how many sequences share each weight stream and how much accelerator memory each sequence holds. The chat-energy calculation showed that the same sharing sets the joules spent per useful token, because each decode step streams the weights once for the whole active batch, so a well-filled batch divides that energy across sequences. Unlike fixed-output inference, LLM energy also grows with response length. Carbon accounting additionally requires an emissions factor and a defined boundary. These per-token bounds describe one accelerator. Deciding how many accelerators a service needs, and what each generated token costs, requires carrying them, together with the fixed-output results of the earlier sections, into capacity planning and unit economics.

## Economics and Planning {#sec-model-serving-economics-capacity-planning-3e7e}

A team that has raised an H100's ResNet-50 throughput several-fold through batching still faces a fleet-level question, namely whether serving a 5,000 QPS target within the same p99 latency SLO costs less on a few H100s or on several times as many lower-cost T4s. Batching, precision tuning, kernel fusion, graph compilation, and the LLM levers that share each weight stream across sequences all improve single-node performance, but production deployment requires choosing how many machines to rent, of what type, and at what total bill. Serving infrastructure cost grows continuously with request volume [@zhang2019mark], while training cost follows a one-time dataset, model, and optimization budget. The bitter lesson sharpens this asymmetry. The methods that win are the ones that scale, so successive models grow larger, and while training pays for that scale once, serving pays for it on every request.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The bitter lesson, that general methods which scale with computation keep outperforming hand-engineered ones, is established in @sec-introduction-bitter-lesson-79c7.
:::

Tail latency dictates the technical design of a serving system, but economics dictates its operational scale. As specialized accelerators and runtime optimizations reduce the compute cycles required per forward pass, the marginal cost per inference declines.[^fn-jevons-paradox-efficiency] Counterintuitively, reduced unit cost does not shrink aggregate serving expenditures. In accordance with Jevons paradox, lower marginal costs stimulate disproportionately higher query volumes, integrating model evaluation deeper into user-facing product loops. At hyperscale, recurring operational inference costs quickly eclipse one-time offline training investments, shifting the primary systems bottleneck toward sustained per-query efficiency.

[^fn-jevons-paradox-efficiency]: **Jevons paradox**\index{Jevons paradox!inference demand}: William Stanley Jevons observed in 1865 that efficiency improvements in coal-powered steam engines increased total coal consumption by making steam power economically viable for applications previously too costly [@jevons1865coal]; the same dynamic can apply to AI inference, where each 10$\times$ cost reduction opens application classes that were economically infeasible at the previous price point, expanding aggregate demand by more than the efficiency gain.

::: {#exmp-model-serving-facebook-inference-tax .callout-example title="Inference cost at Facebook"}

**Scenario**: Production ML serving systems at Meta execute tens of trillions of inferences daily across global user-facing services [@hazelwood2018].

**Diagnosis**: Recurring inference serving compute and energy costs dwarf initial offline model training expenses. Live request arrival patterns and strict latency bounds constrain GPU batching.

**Systems lesson**: Model architectures cheap to train can prove unviable to serve at fleet scale. Production serving infrastructure requires hardware-software co-design to balance tail latency, batch size, and recurring operational total cost of ownership.

:::

The same serving-economics pressure appears in public API prices. @Fig-intelligence-deflation tracks this cost collapse across representative public API list-price snapshots from 2023 through 2025 on a logarithmic scale. The steep downward trend line isolates how prompt token pricing fell by multiple orders of magnitude, from thirty dollars per million tokens for original GPT-4 down to several cents for Gemini 1.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3. Vendor prices change frequently, so these points should be read as historical provenance for the trend rather than as current purchasing guidance [@openai2023chatgptwhisper; @openai2023gpt4web; @openaiCommunity2024gpt4oApi; @openai2024gpt4oMini; @anthropic2024claude3family; @google2024gemini15flashPricing; @deepseek2024v3]. Each order-of-magnitude drop changes which applications are economically viable, and a provider can sustain such prices only if its serving stack extracts more completed requests from each accelerator-hour. Converting engineering efficiency into unit cost draws on the latency, batching, and memory mechanisms of the preceding sections.

::: {#fig-intelligence-deflation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Intelligence Deflation**: Representative public API input-token list prices per 1M tokens (\$) over time (Log Scale). Nine model-version list prices come from the launch and pricing announcements of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and DeepSeek between late 2022 and 2025; the dashed line is a log-linear fit through the price floor, the points that each set a new low. The series is intended as a market trend indicator, not a controlled or current-price comparison. API token-processing prices have collapsed by multiple orders of magnitude, transforming the economics of automated AI workflows." fig-alt="Log-scale scatter plot of nine public API input-token list prices from late 2022 to early 2025, ranging from 30 dollars to 0.075 dollars per million tokens. Blue points are labeled by model, and a red dashed trend line fitted through the cheapest price at each date slopes downward across the plot."}

def _year(iso):

data = sorted((_year(r["date"]), r["usd_per_mtok_input"], r["model"]) for r in Literature.Series.LlmApiInputPrices.entries)

floor = np.minimum.accumulate(prices)

line_prices = 10 ** (slope * line_years + intercept)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

ax.scatter(years, prices, s=45, color=COLORS['BlueLine'], edgecolors='white', zorder=3)
